chunks.content: Introduction Essential hypertension is one of the most common cardiovascular risk factors, affecting 43% to 58% of adults worldwide. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and ventricular remodelling caused by hypertension are the leading causes of cardiovascular death and disability. Unfortunately, the blood pressure control rates required for hypertension treatment is low and the pathogenesis of hypertension is not fully understood. , Periodontitis is another common disease that affects more than half of the global population. Approximately 10% of the population is affected by severe periodontitis. Recently, epidemiological surveys have found that patients with periodontitis have higher blood pressure levels than those with healthy periodontium. Periodontitis is also considered to be one of the factors contributing to a poor antihypertensive effect and a low rate of blood pressure control among patients with hypertension. A meta-analysis has shown that periodontitis can increase the risk of hypertension, especially in patients with severe periodontitis. Using blood pressure as the primary outcome variable, our randomized controlled trial on periodontitis treatment showed that intensive periodontal therapy alone (without antihypertensive medication) effectively reduced blood pressure , the finding that aligns with a 2020 meta-analysis. It has been suggested that periodontitis may be a new factor contributing to the development of hypertension, with the condition labelled ‘dental hypertension’. However, the mechanism by which periodontitis causes elevated blood pressure is unknown. , MMPs are a family of Zn 2+ /Ca 2+ -dependent peptide chain endonucleases that breakdown almost all proteins in the extracellular matrix (ECM) and play a critical role in tissue remodelling. MMPs together with tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) maintain ECM stability. MMP-9 is a member of the MMP family, which was previously found to be associated with cardiovascular remodelling in cardiovascular diseases. Recently, MMP-9 has been found to be associated with hypertension. For example, serum MMP-9 levels are significantly higher in prehypertensive and hypertensive patients than in individuals with normal blood pressure. Our previous experiments showed that injecting exogenous MMP-9 into rats could significantly increase their blood pressure. In periodontitis patients, previous studies have revealed elevated levels of MMP-9 in the gingival tissue and gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) and the local application of nonspecific MMP inhibitors was observed to alleviate periodontitis. , , In terms of the systemic effects, it has been found that serum MMP-9 levels in periodontitis patients are significantly higher than those with healthy periodontum. Likewise, serum MMP-9 levels and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in hypertensive patients with periodontitis were found to be significantly higher than those in patients with simple hypertension. However, whether lowering the serum MMP-9 level can reduce blood pressure in patients with periodontitis is not yet clear. JNJ0966 is a specific MMP-9 inhibitor that reduces both the precursor and the active form of MMP-9. Its high specificity allows it to have almost no effect on the activity of other MMPs. JNJ0966 has been used in in vivo and in vitro studies and has shown good specific inhibition of MMP-9. , The primary aim of this study is to elucidate whether elevated serum MMP-9 constitutes a causal factor underlying the increase in arterial blood pressure in periodontitis and to explore the potential mechanism linking periodontitis, serum MMP-9 elevation and hypertension. Materials and methods Experimental periodontitis animal model construction and MMP-9 inhibitor intervention experiment Thirty-six 12-week-old male SHRs, weighing 249 to 280 g, were purchased from Beijing Viton Lihua Experimental Animal Technology Co., Ltd., license number SCXK 2016-0006 and kept in individually ventilated cages (temperature 22 ± 3 °C, humidity 60%, 12 hours light/dark cycles) at the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Pharmaceutical University Experimental Animal Centre. Six animals were housed per cage and supplied with sufficient food and water. After 1 week of acclimatisation feeding (ie, 13th week of age), 36 animals were randomly by means of a raffle method, divided into the experimental periodontitis group (SHR-L, n = 18) and nonperiodontitis group (SHR-C, n = 18). The experimental periodontitis rat model was induced using a previously reported method, where animals were fasted for 12 hours before the modelling procedure and 3% pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg, intraperitoneal injection) was used for anaesthesia. The SHR-L group was subjected to ligation of the maxillary first and second molars bilaterally with a 4-0 silk thread in an “8” shape. The silk thread was pressed into the gingival sulcus at the cervical region of the teeth. If the silk thread was dislodged, it was religated until the end of the experiment. The SHR-C group was anaesthetised in the same way but without molar ligation. At 4 weeks postmodelling, the rats in both groups were randomly divided into 3 subgroups and were administered JNJ0966 (Selleck) by gavage once per day for 7 days. JNJ0966 was dissolved in 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (Sigma) and was not administered to the SHR-C-0 and SHR-L-0 groups. The JNJ0966 solution was administered at a dose

The SHR-C group was anaesthetised in the same way but without molar ligation. At 4 weeks postmodelling, the rats in both groups were randomly divided into 3 subgroups and were administered JNJ0966 (Selleck) by gavage once per day for 7 days. JNJ0966 was dissolved in 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (Sigma) and was not administered to the SHR-C-0 and SHR-L-0 groups. The JNJ0966 solution was administered at a dose of 10 mg/kg for the SHR-C-10 and SHR-L-10 groups and 30 mg/kg for the SHR-C-30 and SHR-L-30 groups ( n = 6 for each group). Noninvasive tail artery manometry (Anhui Zhenghua Biological Instrument Equipment Co., Ltd) was used to measure SHR systolic blood pressure (SBP). Manometry was performed in the morning at a constant temperature (36-38 °C) in a quiet light-protected cage, systolic blood pressure was measured 3 times and the mean value was calculated. Blood pressure and body weight were measured before modelling and weekly after surgery. After 1 week of JNJ0966 intervention, the rats were anaesthetised again as previously described. Whatman #3 filter paper was cut into 10 × 1 mm strips and 6 strips were randomly selected and placed into marked EP tubes and weighed. Physical isolation with cotton rolls, combined with continuous suction and air-drying, ensures that the fluid collected on the paper strip originates from the gingival crevice and is not diluted or contaminated by saliva. The preweighed filter paper strips were placed into the gingival sulcus of the buccolingual sides of the left first molar for 30 seconds. After removal, all 6 filter papers were placed into the original EP tube. The difference between the 2 weights was the weight of the tooth’s GCF. A blunt-tipped periodontal probe was used to probe the bottom of the gingival sulcus along the surface of the left first molar by a single experienced periodontists (Qianbing Zhou) and the depths of 6 points were measured (mesio-buccal, mid-buccal, disto-buccal, mesio-lingual, mid-lingual and disto-lingual). The values of each point were averaged to measure the probe depth (PD). Similarly, a blunt-tipped periodontal probe was used to lightly probe the gingival sulcus or the bottom of the periodontal pocket and the degree of bleeding was observed 30 seconds after removing the probe. The bleeding was scored on a scale from 0 to 5 to obtain the bleeding index (BI). After the PD and BI measurements, approximately 5 mL of blood was collected from the abdominal aorta with a vacuum blood collection tube with a red top. The blood was then left for 2 hours and centrifuged at 3000 r/min for 15 minutes at 4 °C and the upper layer of serum was collected and stored at −80 °C. The gingival tissue around the left first molar of each SHR was taken, treated with liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. The left first molar and surrounding alveolar bone were collected, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 48 hours, decalcified in 4% hydrochloric acid for 7 days (decalcification endpoint confirmed by needle probing), rinsed under flowing water for 8 hours, embedded in paraffin and longitudinally sectioned along the mesiodistal axis for histopathological examination. MMP-9 and TIMP-1 level measurements and histopathology of SHR alveolar bone All −80 °C frozen specimens were thawed at room temperature (20-25 °C). The GCF was added to 200 μL of Tris-HCl solution (pH 7.5, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd) per tube, shaken for 1 hour and centrifuged at 10,000 r/min for 10 minutes at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected as GCF solution. The GCF solution and serum MMP-9, TIMP-1 and Ang II concentrations were measured using an ELISA kit (R&D Systems) and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio was calculated. The SHR gingival tissue was cut into smaller pieces with ophthalmic scissors and RIPA protein lysis solution (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology) was added to extract the total protein. The total protein concentration of the tissue samples was quantified using a BCA protein concentration quantification kit (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology) on the preformulated SDS‒PAGE electrophoresis gel lane. After electrophoresis, the separated proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore Corporation) and blocked with protein sealing solution (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology) to prevent nonspecific binding of proteins. Next, the PVDF membranes were incubated with primary antibody (MMP-9 protein, Abcam and β-actin, Abcam), overnight at 4 °C on a shaker, then incubated with secondary antibody (Guangzhou AKEA Biotechnology company) for 1 hour on a shaker at room temperature. Finally, the proteins were incubated with chemiluminescence enhancement reagents (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology). After sectioning the alveolar bone tissue, haematoxylin-eosin staining was performed. Image-Pro Plus 6.0 image analysis software (Media Cybernetics, Inc. Version 6.0.0.260) was used to

The BAr/Tar ratio can reflect the degree of bone resorption and destruction of the alveolar bone ( ). Statistical analysis All experimental data were statistically analysed using SPSS 25.0 software. The normality of the data was first tested with Shapiro-Wilk normality test. Data conforming to a normal distribution were presented as the mean ± standard deviation ( ¯X ± SD). Data not conforming to a normal distribution were summarised as the median. The numerical variables of the 2 groups were compared using the independent samples t test or Mann-Whitney U test. For the identification of differences between 2 or more groups of quantitative data, 1-way ANOVA was used if there was homogeneity of variance. The LSD method was used for 2-way comparisons and the nonparametric rank sum test was used if there was no homogeneity of variance. Pearson correlation analysis was used to evaluate correlations. Statistical differences were denoted as P <0.05. Results The weight of the SHRs gradually decreased and blood pressure gradually increased in the periodontitis group during the modelling process. There were no differences in the baseline body weight and blood pressure between the 2 groups at 13 weeks of age. After modelling, the weight of the SHR-C group gradually increased over time, whereas the weight of the SHR-L group decreased at 14 weeks of age and increased again at 15 weeks but remained lower than that of the SHR-C group ( P < 0.0001). The blood pressure of the SHR-L group increased at 14 weeks of age and was significantly higher than that of the SHR-C group at 15 weeks ( P = 0.0198, ). Blood pressure was significantly higher in SHRs with periodontitis than in SHRs without periodontitis and JNJ0966 reduced blood pressure and body weight, especially in the periodontitis group. After 1 week of JNJ0966 intervention, there was no significant difference in body weight between the SHR-L-0 and SHR-C-0 groups, but both the SHR-C-30 and SHR-L-30 groups had lower body weights than the SHR-C-0 and SHR-L-0 groups, respectively ( P = 0.0494, A). Blood pressure was significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group and significantly lower in the SHR-C-30 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0230, B). Blood pressure values in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were significantly lower than those in the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0096 and P = 0.0075, B). The PD, BI and GCF weight were significantly increased in the periodontitis group compared with the nonperiodontitis group. The JNJ0966 intervention did not significantly alleviate these periodontitis-induced increases. The PD, BI and GCF weights were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0115, P = 0.0210 and P = 0.0093), but they were not significantly different between the subgroups within the SHR-C and SHR-L groups after 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966 ( P > 0.05, C-E). Alveolar bone destruction was obvious in the periodontitis group and the JNJ0966 intervention did not significantly reverse this damage. Histopathological examination of the alveolar bone showed that bone destruction and resorption in the SHR-L group were significant compared with those in the SHR-C group and the BAr/TAr (%) ratio was significantly decreased ( P < 0.0001). In contrast, no significant changes were observed in the BAr/TAr (%) ratio of the alveolar bone after 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966 ( P > 0.05, ). Serum MMP-9 levels and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the periodontitis group than in the nonperiodontitis group and were significantly decreased after JNJ0966 intervention. The serum MMP-9 concentration and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0471 and P = 0.0136). Compared with those in the SHR-C-0 group, the GCF MMP-9 concentration and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0086 and P = 0.0025). After 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966, the differences in the GCF MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio between the SHR-C subgroups were not statistically significant. However, the GCF MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratios in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were both significantly decreased ( P = 0.0302 and P = 0.0188) compared with those in the SHR-L-0 group, while the MMP-9 level tended to decline ( F and G). MMP-9 levels were significantly higher in the gingival tissue of the periodontitis group and significantly decreased after JNJ0966 intervention.. Western blot assays showed that the gingival tissue MMP-9 protein level was significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0034). After intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966, the changes in the MMP-9 protein concentrations in the gingival tissues of the SHR-C subgroups were not statistically significant. After JNJ0966 intervention, the MMP-9 concentrations in the gingival tissues of the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were significantly decreased compared with those of the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0077 and P = 0.0055; A and B). Discussion Although epidemiological and clinical studies have found an association between periodontitis and hypertension, the mechanism underlying this relationship is not yet fully elucidated. Previous studies have primarily indicated that systemic immune abnormalities, triggered by local inflammatory lesions associated with periodontitis, may lead to immune-mediated damage to both the kidneys and arterial system. This process also involves the production and release of vasoconstrictive active substances, such as the activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. Furthermore, inflammatory mediators may contribute to endothelial damage and potentially induce the production of specific microRNAs, resulting in cardiovascular remodelling. However, the specific substances involved in these processes remain incompletely understood. , , In this study, an SHR model was successfully established and SHRs with periodontitis were found to have significantly higher arterial blood pressure than control SHRs. This finding is in support of the hypothesis that periodontitis can elevate blood pressure in rats. Given that periodontitis can increase blood pressure, elevated MMP-9 levels in periodontal tissue and serum are often observed in patients with periodontitis and MMP-9 expression may increase blood pressure, we hypothesised that elevated blood pressure in periodontitis patients may, in part, be related to elevated serum MMP-9 levels. However, there is a lack of direct evidence to support this assertion. Given that periodontitis can increase blood pressure, elevated MMP-9 levels in periodontal tissue and serum are often observed in patients with periodontitis and MMP-9 expression may increase blood pressure, we hypothesised that elevated blood pressure in periodontitis patients may, in part, be related to elevated serum MMP-9 levels. However, there is a lack of direct evidence to support this assertion. In this study, by comparing serum MMP-9 levels in SHR with and without periodontitis, we found that serum MMP-9 levels were significantly higher in rats with periodontitis. Importantly, the MMP-9-specific inhibitor (JNJ0966) significantly reduced serum MMP-9 levels and simultaneously lowered arterial blood pressure. This finding provides the first direct experimental evidence that elevated serum MMP-9 is a mechanistic link between periodontitis and hypertension. This study used a silk thread ligation method reported in the literature to induce experimental periodontitis in SHRs and found that compared with the nonperiodontitis control group (SHR-C-0 group), the periodontitis model control group (SHR-L-0 group) had a significantly higher PD and BI and significantly increased GCF weight. The pathological sections showed more alveolar bone and resorption destruction, which is consistent with previous reports. , These observations are also similar to those of human periodontitis, suggesting successful periodontitis modelling. The MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in the GCF of the SHR-L-0 group were significantly higher than those of the SHR-C-0 group. The MMP-9 protein level in the gingival tissues of the SHR-L-0 group was also significantly higher than that of the SHR-C-0 group by Western blot. The MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in the serum of the SHR-L-0 group were significantly higher than those of the SHR-C-0 group. These results are similar to the previous clinical studies of periodontitis patients, , , and thus, this model is considered a suitable model for further exploring the role of MMP-9 in periodontitis-induced hypertension. TIMP-1 inhibits the activity of MMP-9 and the effect of MMP-9 is enhanced when the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio is increased . The current study found that the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio was significantly increased in both GCF and serum, so the net effect of MMP-9 was enhanced in SHRs with periodontitis. To further confirm that increased serum MMP-9 levels are a factor in the elevated blood pressure observed in periodontitis model rats, a specific systemic MMP-9 inhibitor intervention was used in SHRs with and without periodontitis. The results revealed that the periodontitis group showed a significant decrease in GCF and serum MMP-9 levels and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratios and a significant reduction in MMP-9 in gingival tissue after MMP-9 inhibitor intervention. Importantly, a significant decrease in overall blood pressure followed. Correlation analysis showed that the serum MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were moderately correlated with blood pressure, respectively. This finding confirms that elevated serum MMP-9 is 1 factor that contributes to elevated blood pressure in SHR with periodontitis. The benefits of the systemic application of MMP inhibitors in the adjuvant treatment of periodontal disease have been confirmed. For example, low-dose oral doxycycline at a nonantibacterial concentration can significantly reduce the MMP concentration in the periodontal tissue and GCF, which is significantly positively correlated with improvement in the periodontal tissue and alveolar bone destruction. Therefore, orally administered, low-dose doxycycline is recognised as one of the nonsurgical treatments for periodontal disease. However, the efficacy of the systemic application of MMP inhibitors in the treatment of periodontitis combined with hypertension has rarely been reported. The results of this study provide direct evidence for the systemic use of MMP-9-specific inhibitors in the treatment of elevated blood pressure in periodontitis. There are few reports on the effect of increased MMP-9 on blood pressure. , The serum Ang II level in the SHR-L-0 group was significantly higher than that in the SHR-C-0 group. Following the JNJ0966 intervention, with a decrease in serum MMP-9 levels, the serum Ang II levels in the SHR-L-10, SHR-L-30 and SHR-C-30 groups were all significantly lower than those in the corresponding nonintervention groups. This finding suggests that MMP-9 may elevate blood pressure by increasing Ang II levels in serum, as previously reported. However, the mechanism is unknown and it is speculated that it may operate similarly to angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), such as elevating ACE levels so that more Ang I can be converted to Ang II. In addition, MMP-9 interacts with reactive oxygen radicals to increase the secretion of vasoconstrictive substances, such as endothelin-1 and phenylephrine and decrease endothelial nitric oxide production, reducing endothelial diastole function mediated by diastolic substances. This process results in increased vasoconstriction and blood pressure. MMP-9 can breakdown the ECM and cause migration of vascular smooth muscle cells, leading to vascular remodelling, especially thickening of the arterial wall, which causes an increase in vascular resistance. However, to determine whether MMP-9 has a direct vasoconstrictive effect, further studies are needed. Significant decreases in the serum MMP-9 level and blood pressure were also observed in the nonperiodontitis group with high-dose JNJ0966, which may be because SHR itself increased MMP-9 levels. In the present study, the decreases in serum MMP-9 and blood pressure in the periodontitis group after intervention with an MMP-9 inhibitor did not show significant dose dependence. This phenomenon may be due to a higher dose of JNJ0966 in the ‘low-dose’ group and an insufficient dose in the ‘high-dose’ group. Combined with the fact that the high-dose MMP-9 inhibitor subgroup of the nonperiodontitis group exhibited more significant decreases in serum MMP-9 levels and blood pressure compared to those in the low-dose MMP-9 inhibitor group, it can be speculated that there is a dose-dependent relationship between the MMP-9 inhibitor and the reductions in serum MMP-9 levels and blood pressure. In this study, the MMP-9 levels in GCF were significantly decreased in the periodontitis group after intervention with JNJ0966, but periodontitis indices such as the PD value, BI score, GCF weight and BAr/TAr (%) ratio did not significantly improve. There are several possible reasons for these results. First, the periodontal ligature silk thread was not removed and local irritation persisted, which could lead to the continued progression of periodontitis. Second, other MMPs were not inhibited and it has been shown that there are multiple MMPs are highly expressed in the GCF of periodontitis patients. Third, other inflammatory factors, such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α and NF-κB, were not blocked, aggravating alveolar bone destruction and resorption. , Finally, the intervention time was short and the repair of alveolar bone may take longer. Therefore, this result does not demonstrate that the systemic application of MMP inhibitors is ineffective in the treatment of periodontitis. It should be noted that since the silk ligature that induced periodontitis remained in place throughout the experiment, this study could not objectively evaluate the effect of systemic MMP-9 inhibitor application on periodontitis itself. Furthermore, this study only investigated the role of MMP-9 in odontogenic hypertension by treating an experimental periodontitis model in rats with MMP-9 specific inhibitors. As this was not naturally occurring periodontitis, whether differences exist compared to clinically occurring odontogenic hypertension remains unclear, which requires further observation and confirmation in individuals with naturally occurring periodontitis. The reason for the increase in serum MMP-9 levels in individuals with periodontitis is not fully understood. Although previous studies and this study have both found that MMP-9 in the GCF of periodontitis individuals is significantly increased, no significant correlations between the levels of MMP-9 in GCF and serum have been observed. , It can be seen that the increased MMP-9 in serum is not caused by the direct infiltration of high concentrations of MMP-9 into the blood but is more likely to be a systemic reaction to periodontitis. Previous studies have suggested that periodontitis causes a systemic chronic inflammatory response with upregulated expression of proinflammatory factors and this stimulates inflammation-related gene expression and increases the number of inflammatory cells. , , Moreover, Porphyromonas gingivalis can directly enter the blood circulation and invade the vascular wall, aggravating and activating inflammatory cells and monocytes. The antigen of P. gingivalis enhances the immune activity of the patient and activates the immune system and macrophages. Inflammatory cells, macrophages and immune cells can promote MMP-9 secretion, , increasing serum MMP-9 levels. It has been found that the blood neutrophils of patients with periodontitis are significantly increased, and neutrophils are inflammatory cells rich in MMP-9. Because serum MMP-9 is not primarily derived from the osmosis of periodontal fluid, the effect of simple local periodontal treatment on blood pressure is not satisfactory. , In this study, systemic application of MMP-9 inhibitors significantly decreased the serum MMP-9 level and resulted in a significant decrease in blood pressure. This offers a novel approach for lowering blood pressure in hypertensive patients with periodontitis. This finding may help to improve the rate of antihypertensive achievement in patients with refractory hypertension complicated by periodontitis. Of course, this study is based on animal models and must be further confirmed in human patients. Conclusion Serum MMP-9 levels were higher in SHRs with periodontitis than in those without periodontitis. Specific inhibition of MMP-9 reduced blood pressure in SHRs with experimental periodontitis, suggesting that elevated serum MMP-9 levels may be one of the mechanisms underlying elevated blood pressure in individuals with periodontitis. T-cell engager (TCE) therapies are bispecific or multispecific antibodies that simultaneously bind a T-cell receptor complex (usually CD3) and a tumor-associated antigen on target cells, thereby redirecting cytotoxic T cells to recognize and kill tumor cells. TCEs have significantly improved the prognosis of patients with hematologic malignancies and are being explored in solid tumors, resulting in expanding clinical indications. TCEs are now approved for several B-cell and plasma-cell malignancies, including blinatumomab for B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia; teclistamab, talquetamab, and elranatamab for multiple myeloma; and glofitamab and epcoritamab for B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas. , Other agents, such as cevostamab, are under advanced clinical investigation. Compared with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, TCEs are “off-the-shelf” biologics that can be administered immediately without patient-specific cell manufacturing, offering broader accessibility and facilitating integration into clinical practice. However, like other immune-based therapies, TCEs have important treatment-related toxicities, including cytokine-release syndrome (CRS), immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), infusion-related reactions, systemic infections, cytopenias, and tumor flare reactions. Although cardiovascular complications following other immunotherapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors or CAR T-cell therapy, are well described (reported prevalence 0.4%-2.0% and 14.0%-18.0%, , respectively), data on cardiovascular complications associated with TCE therapy are scarce. Recently, Sayed et al described bispecific TCE therapy–related cardiovascular adverse events using the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). However, FAERS is limited by reporting bias and does not capture all drug-exposed individuals, precluding accurate incidence estimation or causal inference. In this retrospective study, we aimed to describe the frequency of cardiovascular complications and baseline factors associated with these events in a large cohort of patients with cancer treated with TCE therapy. Methods Study design This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with a cancer diagnosis who received TCE therapy between January 2016 and December 2024 at 2 large cancer centers: the Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB) Health System and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The study protocol was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board, and the requirement for informed consent was waived given the retrospective nature of this study. Study population We queried the MGB Research Patient Data Registry to identify adult patients with cancer (≥18 years) who initiated their first course of Food and Drug Administration–approved bispecific TCE therapy (blinatumomab, teclistamab, talquetamab, elranatamab, glofitamab, epcoritamab) between January 2016 and December 2024, including both research and nonresearch use. Patients who received at least 1 full dose of TCE therapy were included. The electronic medical records of those identified were manually reviewed (O.I.B.Z., A.N.) to obtain demographic and clinical data (including TCE therapy–related complications and management), as well as laboratory and imaging data. Definition of individual cardiovascular events Left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction was defined as either: 1) a new reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of ≥10 percentage points from baseline to an LVEF <50%; or 2) a new reduction in LVEF of <10 percentage points from baseline to an LVEF of 40% to 49% with either a new relative decline in LV global longitudinal strain (GLS) of >15% from baseline or a new rise in cardiac biomarkers. , Because LV GLS and troponin measurements at baseline and during active therapy were infrequently obtained in our cohort, LV dysfunction was effectively defined by criterion 1 (a new reduction in LVEF of ≥10 percentage points from baseline to an LVEF <50%). Symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was defined as LV systolic dysfunction accompanied by symptoms of heart failure (dyspnea and/or orthopnea). Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was defined as at least 1 heart failure symptom (dyspnea and/or orthopnea) plus 1 or more objective signs of volume overload (chest imaging with pulmonary infiltrates and/or pulmonary edema and/or N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide above the normal range) that responded to loop diuretics. Atrial arrhythmia events were defined as new-onset atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter (AF) or known AF complicated by rapid ventricular response requiring intravenous rate control or pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion. Supraventricular tachycardia included atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia or atrial tachycardia and was considered a cardiovascular event when associated with rapid ventricular response requiring intravenous rate control or pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion. Ventricular arrhythmias were defined as ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. High-degree atrioventricular conduction disease was defined as second-degree Mobitz II or third-degree atrioventricular block on a 12-lead electrocardiogram. Acute coronary syndrome was defined per the 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (AHA) guideline for the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome. Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) and transient ischemic attack (TIA) were defined per the 2021 AHA/American Stroke Association guideline for the prevention of stroke. TCE therapy–related complications CRS and ICANS were graded according to the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy consensus criteria ( ). Clinical covariates Preexisting cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular risk factors were extracted by manual chart review, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, current or former smoking (self-report), AF, prior CVA/TIA, HFrEF, light-chain (AL) amyloid cardiomyopathy, and obstructive coronary artery disease (defined as diameter stenosis of 50% or more in the left main coronary artery or stenosis of 70% or more in a major epicardial vessel). AL amyloid cardiomyopathy was defined by Congo red–positive endomyocardial biopsy or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging findings compatible with amyloid infiltration in the presence of AL amyloid deposits confirmed by a positive Congo red stain and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry typing in a different organ. Established cardiovascular disease was defined as baseline AF, coronary artery disease, CVA/TIA, and/or HFrEF. Cardiac testing was performed at the discretion of the treating clinician and was not prespecified. Echocardiographic variables (LVEF, LV GLS, pericardial effusion [included if more than trivial]) were collected at baseline and during TCE therapy based on the formal interpretations documented in the echocardiography reports. Inflammatory biomarkers before and during TCE therapy were drawn per institutional protocols; peak values were identified. Biomarkers included C-reactive protein (normal reference range 0-3 mg/L), interleukin-6 (normal reference range <7.1 pg/mL), and ferritin (normal reference range 30-400 μg/L). Study outcomes Cardiovascular events and survival were assessed during TCE therapy, defined as the interval from the first TCE dose to 90 days after the last TCE dose. Cardiovascular events were defined as a composite of new LV systolic dysfunction with or without symptomatic heart failure (HFrEF), HFpEF, acute coronary syndrome, AF, clinically significant supraventricular tachycardias, ventricular arrhythmias, high-degree atrioventricular conduction disease, and TIA/CVA. Other outcomes of interest included individual cardiovascular events, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular mortality. Mortality status and cause of death (cardiovascular vs other) were determined from the electronic medical record or death certificates, where available. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were reported as median (25th-75th percentiles [Q1-Q3]) and categorical variables as frequencies and proportions. Baseline characteristics were summarized descriptively without formal hypothesis testing between groups because of informative censoring in the time-to-event framework. Paired comparisons of LVEF and GLS between baseline and during active therapy were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Follow-up was assessed using restricted mean follow-up time because the reverse Kaplan-Meier curve did not reach 50% and median follow-up could not be estimated. For time-to-event analyses, restricted mean time to first cardiovascular event (restricted mean time to failure) was calculated as a measure of average event-free time during the active TCE treatment period with CIs estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations). Cumulative incidence function (CIF) curves were generated using the Aalen-Johansen estimator to account for competing risks. Because analyses were restricted to events occurring during TCE therapy, patients who completed therapy without an event were treated as a competing risk rather than censored because they were no longer at risk once treatment ended. CIFs were calculated for the composite cardiovascular events outcome and for all-cause mortality, treating each outcome as a competing event for the other. In a separate analysis, the CIF for cardiovascular mortality was estimated, treating noncardiovascular death as a competing event. Before model construction, collinearity among candidate variables was assessed using variance inflation factors. For analysis of the composite cardiovascular endpoint, known AF with rapid ventricular response events were excluded to reduce misclassification bias. Univariable Fine-Gray models were used to evaluate associations with the composite endpoint; variables with P < 0.05 were considered for multivariable analysis, with age and sex forced into the model. Multivariable Fine-Gray models were constructed using forward stepwise selection guided by the Akaike information criterion (AIC) to minimize overfitting. Fine-Gray model results are presented as the subdistribution HR with 95% CI. Covariates retained in the stepwise procedure were subsequently incorporated as baseline covariates in cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models evaluating cardiovascular events, with CRS and/or ICANS grades ≥2 included as a time-dependent covariate. For all-cause mortality, univariable Cox proportional hazards models were first fitted. Variables meeting the prespecified selection criteria ( P < 0.05, with age and sex forced into the model) were entered into a forward stepwise AIC-guided multivariable Cox model. The composite cardiovascular event endpoint, including known AF with rapid ventricular response, was incorporated as a time-dependent exposure to assess its association with subsequent mortality. Cox model results are presented as the HR with 95% CI.

Results Baseline characteristics The study cohort included 567 patients with cancer who received their first course of TCE therapy between January 2016 and December 2024. Baseline characteristics are shown in . Median age at the first TCE infusion was 67 years (Q1-Q3: 57-75), and 46.0% (n = 261) were female. Among these patients, 8.6% (n = 49) had a history of obstructive coronary artery disease, 15.3% (n = 87) had AF, 7.4% (n = 42) had known HFrEF or amyloid cardiomyopathy, and 3.7% (n = 21) had a history of CVA/TIA. The most common malignancies were multiple myeloma (n = 232, 40.9%), including 13 with concomitant AL amyloidosis, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (n = 202, 35.6%). Overall, 217 (38.3%) patients were previously treated with anthracyclines, 130 (22.9%) with carfilzomib, and 125 (22.0%) with CAR T-cell therapy. Clinical characteristics during TCE therapy The restricted mean follow-up was 248 days (range: 0-973) and the most frequently used TCE agents were CD19-targeting blinatumomab (n = 212, 37.4%) and B-cell maturation antigen–targeting teclistamab (n = 167, 29.5%) ( ). CRS and ICANS occurred in 256 (45.1%) and 46 (8.1%) patients, respectively, and were most frequent during the first cycle of TCE therapy. Grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS occurred in 88 (15.5%) patients. In univariable Cox models, older age, sex, reduced renal function, a history of cardiomyopathy/HFrEF, lower baseline LVEF, prior pomalidomide/thalidomide exposure, anthracycline exposure, and cancer/TCE agent category were each associated with higher on-treatment all-cause mortality ( ). To identify baseline predictors of mortality at the time of TCE initiation, a multivariable Cox model was constructed using forward stepwise selection guided by the AIC, with age and sex forced into the model. In the final multivariable Cox model, teclistamab (HR: 4.10; 95% CI: 1.90-8.84), epcoritamab (HR: 3.95; 95% CI: 1.86-8.40), and prior anthracycline exposure (HR: 2.72; 95% CI: 1.42-5.23) remained independently associated with higher on-treatment mortality along with older age and sex ( ). To assess whether incident cardiovascular toxicity was associated with subsequent mortality risk, a multivariable Cox model was constructed in which the composite cardiovascular event endpoint was incorporated as a time-dependent covariate. The occurrence of a cardiovascular event was associated with subsequent mortality, with event onset conferring nearly a 7-fold increase in hazard (HR: 6.76; 95% CI: 4.19-10.92), independent of age, sex, TCE agent, and prior anthracycline exposure ( , ). Discussion To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically characterize TCE-related cardiovascular complications and their association with all-cause mortality in a large, real-world cohort of patients with hematologic malignancies ( ). In this dual-center cohort of 567 patients treated with TCEs, the cumulative incidence of on-treatment cardiovascular events was 10.4% (95% CI: 8.1-13.1), with LV dysfunction, and AF, representing the most common presentations. Coronary artery disease was the only baseline variable independently associated with cardiovascular events, whereas development of high-grade CRS and/or ICANS was associated with a significant time-dependent increase in cardiovascular risk. Cardiovascular events were, in turn, associated with subsequent all-cause mortality. In addition, prior anthracycline exposure and treatment with teclistamab or epcoritamab were independently associated with higher mortality. Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment and improved survival outcomes. However, off-target immune activation has been associated with adverse cardiovascular events. Acute myocarditis, although rare (0.4%-2%), is a potentially fatal complication of immune checkpoint inhibitors, with reported mortality rates ranging from 5% to 46%. , In contrast, CAR T-cell therapy–related cardiovascular complications occur in 14% to 16% of patients , and primarily include atrial arrhythmias (8%) and HFrEF (8%), with substantially lower cardiovascular mortality rates (0.50%-0.65%). , In a pharmacovigilance analysis of 3,668 systemic adverse events linked to TCE therapy, cardiovascular events comprised a small subset and included heart failure (1.4%), tachyarrhythmias (1.2%), myocarditis (0.2%), pericarditis (0.1%), and sudden death (0.05%). Collectively, data suggest that TCE therapy is associated with a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile relative to other immunotherapeutic modalities. cardiovascular complications occur in 14% to 16% of patients , and primarily include atrial arrhythmias (8%) and HFrEF (8%), with substantially lower cardiovascular mortality rates (0.50%-0.65%). , In a pharmacovigilance analysis of 3,668 systemic adverse events linked to TCE therapy, cardiovascular events comprised a small subset and included heart failure (1.4%), tachyarrhythmias (1.2%), myocarditis (0.2%), pericarditis (0.1%), and sudden death (0.05%). Collectively, data suggest that TCE therapy is associated with a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile relative to other immunotherapeutic modalities. Consistent with this, our findings demonstrate a cumulative incidence of TCE therapy–related cardiovascular events (10.4%), most commonly HFrEF and AF, with cardiovascular mortality remaining rare (0.4%). No cases of TCE-related acute myocarditis were identified on detailed manual chart review. Although our ability to detect subclinical myocardial injury was limited by inconsistent biomarker assessments, clinical suspicion for myocarditis was low. This aligns with observations from large CAR T-cell therapy studies in which CRS and ICANS are common complications and myocarditis has not been reported. , Another notable finding in this cohort was the relatively low cumulative incidence of high-grade CRS or ICANS (16%), a pattern that may reflect contemporary practice characterized by heightened clinical vigilance and early use of targeted anticytokine therapies such as tocilizumab and anakinra. Nevertheless, among patients receiving TCE therapy, development of grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS was associated with more than a 2-fold increase in cardiovascular event risk, mirroring observations from CAR T-cell therapy in which more severe CRS is associated with greater cardiotoxicity. , Together, these findings reinforce the need for close hemodynamic and cardiac monitoring during episodes of significant immune activation. Further research is needed to establish evidence-based surveillance protocols for early detection and management of cardiovascular toxicity in this setting. Established cardiovascular disease was present at baseline in 26% (n = 147) of the cohort, reflecting the growing inclusion of patients with substantial comorbidities undergoing advanced cancer therapies. Although the cumulative incidence of cardiovascular events during TCE therapy was 10.4%, baseline coronary artery disease was independently associated with a higher risk of subsequent cardiovascular events, including acute coronary syndrome. These findings highlight the importance of thorough cardiovascular assessment and optimization in patients with preexisting coronary artery disease before and throughout TCE therapy. Study limitations First, the cohort was drawn from 2 cancer centers, which may limit generalizability. Second, analyses were restricted to on-treatment cardiovascular events; therefore, we cannot comment on longer-term cardiovascular effects associated with TCE therapy. Third, because TCE dosing schedules varied and the study was retrospective, inflammatory and cardiac biomarkers were measured inconsistently, limiting our ability to assess their temporal relationship with cardiovascular events or to detect subclinical myocardial injury or inflammation. Fourth, this study evaluated TCE-related cardiovascular complications over a 10-year period during which treatment protocols, dosing schedules, premedication, and supportive care strategies evolved. Newly approved TCEs and improvements in monitoring and management of immune-related toxicities also may have influenced cardiovascular outcomes over the study period. Conclusions In summary, this study provides the first detailed characterization of cardiovascular toxicity during TCE therapy in a large real-world cohort. Although overall event rates were modest, preexisting coronary artery disease and development of grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS identified patients at substantially higher cardiovascular risk. These events were, in turn, associated with higher mortality, underscoring the clinical relevance of early recognition and coordinated cardio-oncology care. As TCE use continues to expand, prospective studies are needed to refine risk stratification and define evidence-based surveillance and management strategies. Perspectives COMPETENCY IN MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE: In patients receiving TCE therapies, baseline coronary artery disease and development of grade ≥CRS and/or ICANS identify those at heightened cardiovascular risk; cardiovascular events are significantly associated with higher subsequent mortality. Clinicians should incorporate targeted cardiovascular assessment and closer monitoring in patients with preexisting coronary disease, prior anthracycline exposure, or grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS to facilitate timely detection and management of cardiotoxicity. TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: Future prospective studies are needed to establish standardized surveillance protocols and determine whether tailored preventive or therapeutic strategies can improve outcomes in patients treated with TCE therapy. Introduction Type 2 diabetes (T2D) represents a significant public health concern, characterized by a rapidly increasing global prevalence [ ]. Among the severe complications associated with T2D, the heightened risk of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and lower extremity amputation (LEA) is of particular concern. PAD is an atherosclerotic occlusive disease of the lower extremities, constituting a major form of cardiovascular disease that encompasses both coronary heart disease and cerebrovascular disease [ , ]. The prognosis for patients undergoing amputation due to diabetes is poor, with a mortality rate of 48% within the first-year post-amputation, increasing to > 70% within five years [ ]. In a study in the United States, patients requiring amputations incur 3–6-fold longer hospital stays and significantly higher treatment costs than individuals without such interventions [ ]. These conditions severely diminish quality of life and pose a major socioeconomic challenge, reflecting the substantial costs associated with long-term care, rehabilitation, and overarching burden on healthcare systems [ – ]. Recent clinical guidelines underscore the critical importance of comprehensive management strategies, including lipid-lowering therapy, smoking cessation, intensive glycemic control, and blood pressure management, to mitigate the risk of PAD in individuals with diabetes [ – ]. Statins, the cornerstone of lipid-lowering therapy, have markedly reduced cardiovascular risk but leave a substantial residual risk, even with well-controlled low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels [ – ]. This recognition has spotlighted triglycerides as a crucial therapeutic target for addressing residual cardiovascular risk, although pharmacotherapy aimed at triglycerides has produced mixed outcomes. The prevalent dyslipidemia pattern in patients with diabetes is elevated triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and increased small dense LDL-C [ ]. Despite the acknowledged necessity to manage atherogenic dyslipidemia in T2D patients for reducing residual cardiovascular risk, the effectiveness of fenofibrate, a medication targeted at reducing triglyceride levels, remains contentious [ , – ]. Notably, the Fenofibrate Intervention and Endpoint Lowering in Diabetes (FIELD) study and the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD)-Lipid trial did not conclusively demonstrate a protective effect of fenofibrate against major cardiovascular events in the broad diabetic population [ , ]. However, subgroup analyses have indicated that specific subgroups with T2D, particularly patients with significant hypertriglyceridemia and low HDL-C, might benefit from fenofibrate therapy, indicating the potential for personalized treatment approaches. Due to the mixed evidence regarding the effectiveness of fenofibrate and the critical need for effective strategies to reduce the incidence of PAD and LEA among patients with T2D, this study aimed to investigate the real-world effects of fenofibrate on these outcomes. Methods Study design and data sources The Korean National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database was used in this retrospective observational cohort study. In South Korea, the NHIS is mandatory for the entire population of approximately 50 million people and provides comprehensive medical coverage to Korean nationals. The database contains demographic information such as age, sex, area of residence, and all healthcare utilization data including diagnoses, procedures, medication prescriptions, and surgical codes. Details on the database profile are described elsewhere [ ]. The Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Seoul National University Hospital exempted informed consent because the database was provided to the researchers after anonymization (IRB No.2402-115-1514). Study population A total of 2,741,135 patients with T2D was identified from the NHIS Health Examination Database in 2009–2012. Patients with T2D were defined as individuals who had at least one outpatient visit or any hospitalization with a diagnosis using the International Classification of Diseases 10th (ICD-10) revision code for DM (E11–E14) and prescription for antidiabetic agents or fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥ 126 mg/dL on health check-up. The following subjects were excluded: 1) < 20 years of age ( n = 390); 2) without prescription of statin within one year before the index date ( n = 1,854,163); 3) prescribed any fibrate treatment within one year before the index date ( n = 41,435); 4) missing information ( n = 40,147); or 5) PAD or LEA within one year after the index date ( n = 6,541). The final population enrolled in the study ( n = 798,459) was divided into two groups based on their history of concomitant statin and fenofibrate prescriptions: fenofibrate users (fenofibrate user group) and non-users (non-user group). The two groups were matched 1:4 using propensity scores. A caliper was set within the first 4 to 8 digits for nearest neighbor matching. In the final analysis, 22,984 and 91,936 patients were included in the fenofibrate user group and non-user group, respectively (Fig. ). This study compared the occurrence of each clinical outcome between the fenofibrate user group and the non-user group. Follow-up was assessed from the start of the index treatment (starting fenofibrate) until the first occurrence of each outcome, discontinuation of the index treatment for more than four weeks, or the end of the study, whichever came first. Safety-related outcomes included the occurrence of acute kidney injury (N17) and rhabdomyolysis (M62.82) during the observation period and resulting hospitalizations. These outcomes were compared between the two groups. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were described as either mean and standard deviation (SD) or geometric mean with 95% confidence interval (CI) depending on the normality of their distribution. Categorical variables were presented as numbers and percentages. Propensity score (PS) matching was performed to compare the fenofibrate user and non-user group. The PS was determined by calculating the predicted probability of belonging to either the fenofibrate user or non-user group, employing a logistic regression model that included the following covariates: age, sex, body mass index, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, smoking habit (categorized as never smoker, former smoker, and current smoker), alcohol consumption (categorized as a non-drinker, mild drinker, and heavy drinker based on the amount of alcohol consumption per day of 0 g, < 30 g, and ≥ 30 g, respectively), regular exercise (defined as moderate physical activity for ≥ 30 min on ≥ 5 days per week or vigorous physical activity for ≥ 20 min on ≥ 3 days per week), income level (defined as lowest quartile for Q1 and highest quartile for Q4), urban residence, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD, defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] < 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 measured at index year), duration of diabetes (< 5 years or ≥ 5 years), insulin user, oral antidiabetic medication (< 3 classes vs. ≥ 3 classes), fasting blood glucose, total cholesterol, triglyceride, HDL-C, LDL-C, and eGFR. To enhance the robustness of the statistical analysis, each patient in the fenofibrate user group was matched with four patients in the non-user group. The absolute standardized difference (ASD) was used to assess covariate balance, with values of < 0.1 considered indicative of balance. The incidence rate (IR) for each outcome was calculated by dividing number of events by follow-up time (person-years), expressed in units of 1,000 person-years. Cox proportional hazards regression model was used for analysis of the event occurrence risk. The control group, consisting of patients not treated with fenofibrate, was used as the reference group. The hazard ratio (HR) and corresponding 95% CI were calculated. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess whether the risk for primary outcomes was consistent for the fenofibrate user group compared with the non-user group in different subgroups: age < 65 years vs. ≥ 65 years); male vs. female; LDL-C < 100 mg/dL vs. ≥ 100 mg/dL; low HDL-C (40 mg/dL and 50 mg/dL for males and females, respectively) and high triglycerides (150 mg/dL) or not; duration of diabetes < 5 years vs. ≥ 5 years; concomitant CKD (-) vs. (+); and multiple antidiabetic combination treatments with < 3 classes vs. ≥ 3 classes. Cox regression analysis was conducted as the primary analysis after adjustment for potential confounders. Statistical analyses were performed using the SAS software package (SAS version 9.4: SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC, USA). All analyses were considered significant with a two-sided p-value < 0.05 and p for interaction < 0.1. Discussion In this large-scale, population-based nationwide cohort study, the results showed that use of fenofibrate among patients with T2D who had been on statin therapy for > 1 year was associated with significant reductions in the risk of composite outcome by 18.9%, of LEA by 24.2%, and of PAD by 19.1% compared with non-users. Notably, the benefits of fenofibrate were more pronounced in older patients (age ≥ 65 years), those receiving less intensive antidiabetic therapy (< 3 combination therapies), and particularly in individuals with lower triglyceride levels, in which the risk reduction for PAD was most significant. Current national and international guidelines for the management of diabetes recommend the control of modifiable risk factors to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events or major adverse limb events, including peripheral revascularization or major amputation, in patients with PAD [ , , , ]. In a previous systematic review and meta-analysis, statin use was associated with a significant 30% reduction in major adverse limb events and amputations (pooled HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.61–0.82 and pooled HR 0.65; 95% CI 0.52–0.82, respectively) [ ]. Due to the atherogenic dyslipidemia of patients with T2D, fibrates may be a logical therapeutic option for residual risk that is not fully resolved by statins because fibrates have been shown to have beneficial effects on HDL-C, triglycerides, and anti-inflammatory properties [ , – ]. Therapeutic options for PAD have been driven mainly by research on atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases such as coronary heart disease and stroke [ ]. Fenofibrate activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-α, which influences the expression of a variety of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation, lipoprotein lipase synthesis, and reduction of apolipoprotein C-III [ ]. Consequently, fenofibrate effectively lowers plasma triglycerides and raises HDL-C level. Furthermore, fenofibrates have been shown to exhibit anti-inflammatory and antioxidative effects and to improve endothelial function [ – ]. In several previous randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the efficacy of fenofibrate in reducing cardiovascular events was reported in patients with T2D; however, these studies had relatively small sample sizes (ranging from 164 to 769 patients with T2D) [ – ]. In recent large RCTs, fenofibrate failed to achieve statistical significance in the prevention of cardiovascular events [ , ]. The results of FIELD did not significantly differ between the fenofibrate and placebo groups in the primary outcome of coronary heart disease events at five years of follow-up [ ]. However, the secondary outcomes showed a significant reduction of 11% in total cardiovascular events, 21% in coronary revascularization, and 20% in total revascularization. The FIELD study was conducted with T2D patients who were not on lipid-modifying therapy at baseline. By the end of the study, 33.8% (n = 1,657) and 18.2% (n = 890) of the fenofibrate and placebo groups, respectively, had started using statins. This may explain the lack of statistical significance for the primary outcome of the FIELD study. This study is a retrospective cohort study and differs significantly in methodology and study population from the FIELD study, which was an RCT. Specifically, we examined the effect of fenofibrate on PAD and LEA in patients with T2D who had been taking statins for at least one year. In addition, the fenofibrate group in this study had higher median baseline triglyceride levels (235.0 mg/dL, 95% CI 233.4–236.6) compared with fenofibrate users in the FIELD study (153.1 mg/dL, IQR 118.6–203.5), which may explain the more pronounced effect of fenofibrate in reducing PAD and LEA in the present study. The ACCORD-LIPID trial, which is another representative large scale RCT in which the cardiovascular benefits of fenofibrate were compared in patients with T2D on statin, also failed to demonstrate a significant beneficial effect of fenofibrate over placebo for the composite primary outcome of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular mortality [ ]. Although significant interactions were not found between subgroups, the incidence of the primary outcome was lower in the fenofibrate group (12.4%) compared with the placebo group (17.3%) in the subgroup of patients with high triglyceride levels (≥ 204 mg/dL) and low HDL-C levels (≤ 34 mg/dL), indicating that fenofibrate treatment may be beneficial in certain patient populations (p = 0.057 for interaction). In this study, the benefit of fenofibrate on PAD was pronounced in the subgroup with lower triglyceride levels, based on a pre-specified subgroup analysis (p = 0.038 for interaction), supporting the importance of consistently maintaining triglycerides within normal range. In addition, fenofibrate was associated with a significant 25% reduction in the primary outcome in the subgroup taking ≤ 3 oral antidiabetic drugs (OADs; p = 0.011 for interaction). be beneficial in certain patient populations (p = 0.057 for interaction). In this study, the benefit of fenofibrate on PAD was pronounced in the subgroup with lower triglyceride levels, based on a pre-specified subgroup analysis (p = 0.038 for interaction), supporting the importance of consistently maintaining triglycerides within normal range. In addition, fenofibrate was associated with a significant 25% reduction in the primary outcome in the subgroup taking ≤ 3 oral antidiabetic drugs (OADs; p = 0.011 for interaction). In a 4.9-year extension study consisting of the ACCORD-Lipid survivors (ACCORDION), patients receiving a combination of statin and fenofibrate exhibited a 35% improvement in survival compared with subjects treated with statin alone (aHR 0.65; 95% CI 0.45–0.94; p = 0.02) [ ]. Based on subgroup analysis in the present study, this finding indicates a potential ‘legacy effect’ of early fenofibrate intervention, potentially leading to improved outcomes, especially when initiated prior to the progression of diabetes or the requirement for a more complex regimen of OADs for effective glycemic control. Meanwhile, our study showed that the composite outcome of LEA and PAD exhibited a 37.1% reduction in the older patients (age ≥ 65 years), compared to a 9.1% reduction in younger patients (age < 65 years) ( p = 0.021 for interaction). This provides evidence that proactive lipid lowering therapy with fenofibrate and statins could help prevent major adverse limb events, even in older patients with T2D. The present study had several limitations. Because this was a population-based cohort study, challenges existed in establishing causal relationship. Despite PS matching being performed to mitigate confounding factors, the possibility of residual unaccounted biases cannot be entirely excluded. However, the findings either align with or serve as robust supplementary evidence to the trends observed in previous comprehensive clinical studies. Such evidence supports the proactive consideration of fenofibrate as a treatment strategy to mitigate major adverse limb events in particular subsets of patients with diabetes who are concurrently undergoing statin therapy. The dataset used in this study primarily captured the sociodemographic characteristics and health behaviors of the South Korean population, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other ethnicities. An analysis of data from the 2013–2015 Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey revealed a high consumption of carbohydrates, contrasted with low intake levels of meat, fish, eggs, legumes, and dairy products [ ]. This analysis further identified that males with high carbohydrate intake were inclined toward a 1.35-fold higher odds ratio for developing metabolic syndrome, and females with similar dietary patterns exhibited a 1.38-fold higher odds ratio for reduced HDL-C levels. The results of the present study mirror the prevalent carbohydrate-dominant dietary habits in South Korea, potentially influenced by alcohol consumption habits associated with hypertriglyceridemia. Consequently, this underscores a possibility that the effectiveness of fenofibrate is accentuated in populations characterized by high carbohydrate consumption or in ethnic groups with prevalent high alcohol intake [ ]. Conclusions The large-scale real-world evidence in the present study indicated that fenofibrate treatment in individuals with T2D was associated with a reduced risk of major adverse limb events, including LEA and PAD, throughout a median observation period of 7.6 years. These findings highlight the valuable role of fenofibrate in reducing the risk of serious vascular complications associated with atherogenic dyslipidemia in patients with T2D. Introduction Perioperative myocardial injury/infarction (PMI) following noncardiac surgery has been increasingly recognized as a frequent cardiac complication, mostly without typical ischemic symptoms [ – ], which occurs in at least 8% of elective procedures [ , ], and 20% of major surgeries [ ]. Moreover, PMI is independently associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular (CV) morbidity and mortality at 30 days and up to 1 year after noncardiac surgery [ , – ]. Asymptomatic PMI is comparable to symptomatic PMI [ ]. Therefore, strategies to improve the detection of PMI for noncardiac surgical patients may provide major medical benefits [ ]. For early identification of surgical patients at high risk of PMI, attention should be paid to preoperative assessment. The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) is recommended in clinical practice guidelines [ ] and has been widely used to predict perioperative cardiac risk [ – ]. Meanwhile, frailty is an emerging risk factor for major adverse CV events perioperatively among patients undergoing noncardiac surgery [ ]. However, it remained unknown whether the RCRI and frailty could perform well for the prediction of PMI in noncardiac surgery patients under care of the surgical and medical co-management (SMC) model. The complexity of patients undergoing intermediate- or high-risk noncardiac surgery exceeds the capacity of any one surgical group to be managed independently, so patients benefit from a team-based approach to care [ ]. The collaborative model of SMC [ ] is a strategy that emphasizes patient-centered care and aims to optimize the quality of perioperative care and improve survival and postoperative outcomes. Under SMC, internists are proactive involved in all aspects of perioperative care, including preoperative assessment and optimizing perioperative medical therapy, postoperative support and management of complications, and maximizing functional recovery [ ]. Previous studies have reported that the implement of SMC resulted in better outcomes in high-risk orthopedic [ – ], vascular [ ], colorectal surgery [ ] and neurosurgery [ , ], such as reduced medical complications, decreased length-of-stay, reduced in-hospital mortality or one-year mortality [ – ]. The practice of SMC is gaining popularity, as there has been a rapid increase in the percentage of noncardiac surgical patients under SMC, mainly in the United States [ ]. However, little is known about the risk of PMI in intermediate- or high-risk noncardiac surgery patients under care of the SMC model in a real-world clinical setting. The Department of Geriatric Comprehensive Surgery of the author’s team is a perioperative SMC team with 35 years of clinical experience in perioperative management. Thus, in this study, we evaluated PMI risk and explore preoperative assessment tools of PMI in patients at increased CV risk who underwent intermediate- or high-risk noncardiac surgery under care of the SMC model in a real-world clinical setting. Methods Study population This was a prospective cohort study that included consecutive patients at increased CV risk who underwent intermediate- or high-risk inpatient noncardiac surgery at the Second Medical Center, Chinese PLA General Hospital, Beijing, China, between January 2017 and December 2022. Patients were included if they were ≥ 65 years old, or ≥ 50 years old with a history of cardiovascular disease (CVD) or CV risk factors (e.g., smoking, obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia) [ ], treated with intermediate- or high-risk noncardiac surgery according to the criteria of the ESC/ESA surgical risk score [ ] and with a postoperative stay of ≥ 2 days. Plasma concentrations of cardiac troponin (cTn) were measured routinely within 14 days before surgery, on postoperative days 1 and 2, and later if clinically indicated. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) was performed when PMI was detected and whenever indicated clinically. A detailed clinical evaluation for the PMI work-up and therapy was performed when PMI was detected. Patients were excluded if one of the following was met: cardiac surgery or MI within 14 days before admission, surgery involving a cardiac surgeon (e.g., coronary artery bypass graft, heart valve surgery, repair of congenital heart disease, surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, or cardiac transplantation), low-risk noncardiac surgery, no cTn measurement within 14 days before surgery or 3 days after surgery, elevated preoperative cTn level, or lost to follow-up after discharge. Surgical and medical co-management In the Second Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital, the author’s team is a perioperative SMC team with 35 years of clinical experience in perioperative management. The relationship between the surgeon and the internist is a patient-centered collaboration. Under normal conditions, the internist also participates in daily rounds, prescribes medicines, and writes progress notes. All patients were treated by the perioperative SMC team according to the updated clinical guidelines, among which the guidelines for CV assessment and management of patients were inspired by the 2022 ESC guidelines [ ]. All patients were treated by the perioperative SMC team according to the updated clinical guidelines, among which the guidelines for CV assessment and management of patients were inspired by the 2022 ESC guidelines [ ]. It is recommended to routinely measure cTn in patients with an increased CV risk before intermediate- and high-risk noncardiac surgery, and 24 and 48 h thereafter. It is also recommended to obtain a preoperative 12-lead ECG, and measure preoperative brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) concentrations in those patients. As Fig. shows, SMC was initiated when surgical intervention was indicated and throughout the entire perioperative period. Ethics statement This study was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Chinese PLA General Hospital and registered with the ISRCTN registry (reference number: ISRCTN58897355). The study was performed following the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all included patients. Variables and definition The data of the included patients was prospectively collected and recorded. Variables included baseline demographics, concomitant diseases, the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score, perioperative laboratory values such as hemoglobin, creatinine, and cTn, examination indices such as ECG and cardiac ultrasound, type of surgical procedure, surgical information, perioperative medications, and postoperative complications during hospitalization. Thirty-day mortality was determined by phone interview or clinical visit. We calculated the RCRI for each patient to evaluate the risk of cardiac complications. The RCRI [ ] consists of six categorical variables, including a history of ischemic heart disease, history of heart failure, history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, history of cerebrovascular accident or transient ischemic attack (TIA), baseline creatinine ≥ 2 mg/dl, and high-risk surgery (intrathoracic, intra-abdominal, or suprainguinal vascular surgery). One point was given for each variable, and the RCRI score was calculated for each patient by summing all of the points. Patients were divided into four risk classes (I: 0 point; II: 1 point; III: 2 points; IV: ≥ 3 points). Frailty was assessed using the FRAIL Scale [ , ], which consists of a 5-item screening questionnaire with simple “yes” or “no” answers: Fatigue (evaluated by asking patients if they felt tired most of the time), muscle resistance (indicated by a patient’s capacity to climb a flight of stairs), aerobic capacity (evaluated by a patient’s capacity to walk one block independently), illness (evaluated by the presence of five or more diseases), and weight loss (measured by a decline of ≥ 5% within the past 6 months). One point was given for each affirmative response. Scores ranged from 0 to 5 points, and patients were divided into three categories: robust (0 point), prefrail (1–2 points), and frail (≥ 3 points). Outcomes The primary outcome of PMI was a peak plasma concentration of cTn T ≥ 30 ng/L (measured by using an Elecsys System, Roche Diagnostics) within 3 days following noncardiac surgery, independent of symptoms or ECG changes [ , ]. According to the dominant trigger for MI injury, PMI was classified as extra-cardiac (triggered by a primarily extra-cardiac disease, such as severe sepsis, stroke, pulmonary embolism [PE], or surgical trauma) or cardiac (type 1 myocardial infarction [TIMI] caused by plaque rupture, type 2 myocardial infarction [T2MI] caused by a supply-demand mismatch, acute heart failure, or tachyarrhythmia) [ ]. The confirmation and classification of PMI were adjudicated by two independent internists based on all related clinical information. Other postoperative complications (e.g., the Clavien-Dindo classification of surgical complications [ , ]) and thirty-day mortality were also collected. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean with standard deviation (SD) and were compared using Student’s t -test. Categorical variables are reported as numbers with percentages and were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate. Logistic regression analysis was used for univariate and multivariate analyses, with PMI as the dependent variable. Potential predictors of PMI were selected using univariate analysis ( p < 0.1). The potential predictors and other clinically related candidate variables were included in the multivariate analysis, and independent PMI predictors were selected using multivariate forward selection ( p < 0.05). A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was used to evaluate the discriminatory ability of the RCRI, frailty, and their combination to predict PMI. An area under the curve (AUC) > 0.7 was considered to indicate acceptable discriminatory capacity, with AUC ≥ 0.8 considered to indicate excellent discriminatory capacity [ , ]. Calibration was assessed using the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (HL), and p < 0.05 indicated a poor fit. In addition, post-hoc sensitivity analyses were performed. Results Study cohort and baseline characteristics A total of 613 eligible patients were included in this analysis (Fig. ). In total, the mean (SD) age was 73.3 (10.9) years, with 466 patients aged ≥ 65 years (76.0%). Meanwhile, 183 patients had coronary artery disease (CAD) (29.8%), and 51 had undergone a coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (8.4%), of whom 3 patients underwent coronary revascularization (with 1 patient underwent percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty and 2 underwent CABG) before the scheduled surgical procedure as part of the reduction of cardiac risk (0.5%). Moreover, 594 patients (97.0%) received an ECG, and the biomarker BNP was measured before noncardiac surgery in 561 patients (91.5%). In brief, 24 patients (3.9%) had a Clavien-Dindo classification for surgical complications ≥ 3. The overall 30-day mortality rate was 1.7% ( n = 11/613). Incidence and the underlying PMI etiologies PMI occurred in 24/613 patients (3.9%). The underlying PMI etiologies were extra-cardiac in 6/24 (25.0%) patients, TIMI in 5/24 (20.8%) patients, acute heart failure in 4/24 (16.6%) patients, tachyarrhythmia in 5/24 (20.8%), and likely T2MI in 4/24 (16.6%). Risk factors for PMI Patients with PMI were older, had a lower body mass index (BMI) and hemoglobin level, had more CV comorbidities, and had a higher likelihood of ASA status ≥ 3 and emergency noncardiac surgery (Table ). Moreover, the rate of PMI increased with the risk category of the RCRI and FRAIL scale systems (Fig. ). Consequently, patients with PMI had a much higher rate of 30-day mortality than patients without PMI (29.2% vs. 0.7%, p = 0.00). Multivariate regression analysis revealed that frailty (odds ratio [OR] = 5.91; 95% CI, 2.34–14.93; p = 0.00), coronary heart disease (OR = 4.69; 95% CI, 1.75–12.58; p = 0.00), and hemoglobin (OR = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.94–0.99; p = 0.01 were independently associated with PMI (Table ). Ability of the RCRI, frailty, and their combination to predict PMI The calibrated RCRI score, frailty, and their combination were adequate to predict PMI in the whole cohort (HL p > 0.05). The RCRI demonstrated acceptable discriminatory capacity for predicting PMI (AUC, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.67–0.88). Frailty also demonstrated acceptable discriminatory capacity (AUC, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.62–0.86). Combining frailty with the RCRI further increased the AUC to 0.87 (95% CI, 0.81–0.93) for predicting PMI among all patients (Table ). Post-hoc sensitivity analyses The calibrated RCRI score, frailty, and their combination were adequate to predict PMI in all subgroups (HL p > 0.05). The RCRI demonstrated acceptable discriminatory capacity for elderly patients, patients with cardiac diseases, CAD patients, coronary intervention/CABG patients, and those with ASA status ≥ 3 (AUC > 0.7) (Table ). Meanwhile, the RCRI had excellent discriminatory power for subgroups of patients with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and high-risk surgery (AUC ≥ 0.8) (Table ). In addition, frailty showed poor or acceptable discriminatory power for all subgroups (AUC, 0.67–0.74) (Table ). Their combination enhanced the discriminatory power for all subgroups (AUC, 0.78–0.86) versus the RCRI alone (Table ). The discrimination by the RCRI was acceptable or excellent in both settings (patients with high-risk surgery and those with intermediate-risk surgery) (AUC > 0.7) (Table ). Discrimination performance of frailty remained consistent in both settings (AUC > 0.7) (Table ). Their combination also enhanced the discriminatory power for the both settings (AUC > 0.8) (Table ). Whether patients aged ≥ 75 years or not, the discrimination performance of the RCRI, frailty, and their combination for predicting PMI also largely remained consistent with those of the whole cohort (Table ).
