Keywords African relevance • This scoping review highlights the lack of emergency medical dispatch (EMD) research focus within Africa. • To develop emergency medical services (EMS) within Africa it is important to identify the education and training needs for the EMD staff. • The scoping review identifies specific competencies/ characteristics required by EMD staff which can assist in guiding training needs of EMD staff in Africa. Introduction A key part of the healthcare system is an effective Emergency Medical Service (EMS) which responds promptly to individuals who are ill or injured, providing emergency medical care and, when necessary, transporting patients to appropriate healthcare facilities [ ]. The EMS call centre, also known as the Emergency Medical Dispatch (EMD) is critical to the patient journey and can directly affect resource availability and allocation, response time and level of care provided [ , , ]. Reducing EMS response time leads to faster patient arrival at the appropriate healthcare facility, where definitive treatment can be initiated, resulting in decreased mortality and morbidity rates [ , ]. A functional EMD, relies on competent call takers and dispatchers, playing a pivotal role in improving EMS response times by coordinating their efforts, maximizing the chances of a positive outcome for patient’s. Moreover, the ability of EMD staff to provide pre-arrival instructions can significantly impact patient survival rates, particularly in time-critical emergencies such as cardiac arrest or severe injury [ , , , ]. An effective EMD integrates the knowledge and skills of its staff to optimize the utilization of limited resources with the goal of ensuring members of public have access to an EMS in a “timely, safe, locally appropriate, and reliable manner.” [ ] This is ideally accomplished through a well-known universal access number (UAN) where EMD staff use the available resources to address the emergency [ , , ]. To improve EMD many EMS in high-income countries (HIC) have incorporated computer-aided dispatch (CAD) systems with service-specific guidelines and protocols [ , , ]. The primary aim of a CAD system is to assist EMS organizations to efficiently manage incoming calls and dispatch appropriate resources, reducing response times, while providing EMS crews with important information regarding the emergency [ ]. In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), EMD systems lack standardization [ , ], and some EMS have call taking working separately from the dispatch centres, with computer systems that do not function cohesively [ ]. These challenges likely result in EMD in LMICs that rely heavily on the competencies of the individual call takers and dispatchers [ , ]. Although two separate functions, the roles and responsibilities of the call taker and dispatcher are closely intertwined requiring critical competencies to effectively manage emergency calls. A study focusing on the psychological health of EMD staff in Canada, conducted by Toulouse et al [ ] defined competencies as a “stabilized set of knowledge and know-how, standard conduct, standard procedure, types of reasoning that can be applied without new training” and EMD staff competencies as “the knowledge system that allows the activity to be produced that meets the task requirements.” [ ] EMD staff competencies include effective interviewing skills to gather essential information; rapid decision-making abilities; proficiency in dispatch systems and communication tools; possessing medical knowledge to provide telephonic advice; and multitasking to manage and coordinate services [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. These competencies enable EMD staff to effectively manage emergencies, provide pre-arrival instructions, and facilitate timely responses. In many LMICs, there are no minimum EMD requirements, and not all EMS make use of a CAD system. An opportunity exists within LMICs to enhance the quality of EMS call taking and dispatch by identifying existing programs and competency requirements in the literature. Utilizing this literature to determine the gaps in the current competency requirements will inform the path forward identifying ways to address the gaps through focused research. This study reviews existing literature on the competencies of EMD staff and identifies any additional requirements or training, for EMD staff from this body of literature. Methods A scoping review of EMD staff competency requirements was conducted in line with Arksey and O’Malley’s framework which is consistent with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis extension for scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines [ , ]. The development of this scoping review methodology encompassed: (i) identifying the research question, (ii) identifying relevant studies, (iii) study selection, (iv) charting the data, and (v) collating, summarizing, and reporting the results, in alignment with the six stages outlined in the guiding framework. We used the Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework to formulate our research question, and this scoping review therefore asks: “What is known from the existing literature about the competencies required (concept) by EMD (context) staff (population)?”

The search was conducted in January 2025 with the first published article noted in 1983 and included articles up to January 2025. The search strategy ( ) was developed a priori using the following keyword combinations (Emergency Medical Service, EMS call centre, competencies) and their synonyms. The reviewers (WV and CM) agreed on the eligibility criteria and reviewed the titles and abstracts of all identified articles. Both reviewed abstracts independently, and where decisions differed, the reviewers discussed their reasons, and a final decision was agreed upon. Full-text articles were extracted and further analysed to determine whether they aligned with this study. To address the research question, this study included original research articles published in English that focused on individuals employed in EMD (responsible for answering emergency calls, recording call details, and dispatching ambulances), and personnel working in combined fire and ambulance service call centres. Grey literature, when included, comprised published books on EMS call-taking and dispatch, EMS regulations, and unpublished literature accessible through specific EMS websites. We excluded studies where the words ambulance, EMS or fire brigade were not specifically mentioned in the title or abstract. Two reviewers (WV and CM) independently conducted a comprehensive review of the full text articles and extracted pertinent information from each, including the study characteristics (article title, authors, publication year, country of study, research objectives, sample size, potential biases or study limitations, and significant findings) ( ); competency requirements for EMD staff; and education and training requirements specific to EMD. Where no specific competencies were included in an article, competencies were derived from the functions described. Using deductive analysis, the outcomes of the scoping review were categorized into three focus areas: EMD system requirements, EMD staff minimum requirements, and derived competencies of EMD staff. Waiver of ethical clearance was provided by the University of Cape Town (UCT) Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC 745/2023). EMD in-service training To maintain competency, additional in-service training on the use of CAD/ MPDS was highlighted in several studies [ , , , , ]. With regards to specific clinical in-service training, 14 studies focused on training of the EMD staff to recognize and provide advice for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ], three studies looking at the dispatcher’s ability to recognise a patient having a stroke; [ , , ] while one study focused on the classification of emergencies involving the paediatric patient [ ], and a further study looking at the effectiveness of providing first aid instructions in the trauma patient [ ]. In EMD where staff were not required to use prior scripted protocols (CAD/ MPDS), giving EMD staff complete autonomy, studies did show the importance of receiving job-specific training to improve their performance [ , , , , ]. The review of grey literature identified eight specific EMD programs. The programs offered in the USA and Canada were focused on the use of the CAD/ MPDS [ , , ], with programs offered in Taiwan [ ], and Nepal [ ] focusing on interview skills, basic first aid and protocol adherence. EMD programs offered by universities or training academies, leading to a formal qualification in EMD were found in Australia [ ], Belgium [ ] and Finland [ ]. These formal qualifications included modules on effective interview and communication skills, effective use of available technology, medical terminology and first aid, managing stressors in the work environment, effective use of resources, inter-agency communication, workplace health and safety, effective reporting, and feedback. Discussion The aim of the scoping review was to identify existing literature on the competencies of EMD staff and any additional requirements or training, for EMD staff from existing literature. There has been a renewed interest in EMD research during the last five years with 13 articles published of which four focused on LMICs [ , , , ] Despite this renewed interest, evidence suggests that EMD staff competencies are poorly described in the literature and given their importance, we were able to synthesize practices and experiences suggesting core competencies from around the world. It is evident that EMD are well established in HIC, where existing research focuses on the accurate utilization of CAD systems or MPDS [ , , , , , , , ]. The EMD in many LMIC do not use a standardised CAD system increasing the reliance on the EMD staff to identify the emergency and assign a priority, locating the incident and allocating EMS crews that can respond to the emergency. The African Federation for Emergency Medicine (AFEM) in 2013 identified the need to develop EMS systems in Africa taking into consideration unique challenges faced which would include the lack of resources, while cautioning against simply adopting a “western style” EMS system [ ]. The need to develop EMD systems that are suitable to the African healthcare vision will require focused development of EMD staff. Only two studies have directly addressed the competencies of EMD staff [ , ]. This may be because EMD staff are expected to adhere strictly to established guidelines without deviating from these protocols [ , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Another reason may be that EMS has primarily focused on response times and the quality of patient care [ , , ], potentially overlooking the critical role played by the EMD staff who form an integral part of the EMS. A more plausible reason may be that EMD staff in HIC would have exposure to technology prior to employment with the assumption that they have basic knowledge of computer systems, are fairly computer literate and will be working in a well-regulated environment where adherence to standard operating procedures is mandatory. In many LMICs EMD staff may have limited access to technology and will be working within systems that are still developing, requiring a different focus for education and training programs. As early as 1977, Griggs et al [ ]. recognized that medically trained staff were more proficient in assessing the acuity of a patient's condition based on the caller's description and subsequently dispatching appropriate resources. The employment of medically trained personnel is also considered beneficial for fostering relationships with hospital professionals, ensuring accurate relay of medical information from ambulance crews to receiving hospital staff for adequate preparation [ , , , ]. The overburdened and under resources healthcare systems within LMICs raises questions about having nurses or physicians working in the EMD and this expertise are needed elsewhere within the healthcare system. It is noted that the current high rates of over-triaging (>54 % of calls) within the EMD directly impacts the availability of resources [ ]. Providing EMD staff with a comprehensive understanding of medical conditions so that they can pose pertinent, focused questions to gain deeper insights into emergencies, provide medical advice, and dispatch suitable resources is key [ , , , , , , , , ]. Sending ambulances to an incorrect address causes delays in the patient receiving medical care where EMD staff must now trace the original caller, verify information regarding incident location, locating the closest vehicle again so that assistance can be provided. It is therefore necessary to determine what the specific needs of EMD staff with reference to their medical knowledge and expertise and address these through targeted training programs. Whether in HICs or LMICs, EMD staff must possess the ability to adapt to the unique circumstances they will encounter [ , , ]. It is important for EMD staff to have excellent communication skills that include the ability to discern variations in the caller's tone of voice, identify and address language barriers, be sensitive to cultural differences, use appropriate medical terminology, use technology effectively and be able to resolve conflicts effectively [ , , , ]. Addressing the in-service training needs of EMD staff in LMICs requires a distinct approach compared to HICs. This is due to contextual factors such as limited resources, the absence of standardized CAD systems, and underdeveloped road infrastructure, all of which contribute to uncertain response times and necessitate tailored in-service training interventions [ , ]. In LMICs, preventing death involves identifying treatable conditions beyond OHCA, such as infectious diseases, ischemic heart disease (IHD), strokes, and trauma-related emergencies [ , ]. While IHD and stroke remain the leading causes of death [ ], it is equally important to consider other contributing factors in tailoring in-service training. In a country such as South Africa, with rich and diverse cultures, it is equally important to focus in-service training on understanding the different cultures and their understanding of medical emergencies, recognizing language barriers and finding ways to overcome these barriers. In a country such as South Africa, with rich and diverse cultures, it is equally important to focus in-service training on understanding the different cultures and their understanding of medical emergencies, recognizing language barriers and finding ways to overcome these barriers. Alongside these, in-service training must also focus on anatomy and physiology, symptomatology [ ], correctly answering emergency calls and interview techniques [ , , ], effective communication, basic psychology [ ], and effective use of technology, including video calling in an emergency [ , ]. The aim of in-service training needs to enhance EMD staff knowledge and skills in specific areas while simultaneously highlighting the importance of the EMD within the healthcare system. The review of existing training revealed several programs that encompass a variety of competencies relevant to EMD staff that include interview skills, effective teamwork within complex environments, adept use of technology, and basic first aid provision with the use of available technology [ , , , , , , ]. The scoping review shows that, where focused training programs are in place, EMD staff are provided with the requisite competencies (knowledge and skills) required to perform effectively within the healthcare system [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. The capacity to use these competencies effectively, functioning within a team, under exceptional stress, while demonstrating empathy, constitutes an integral component of how the EMS should perform to enhance service delivery with the objective of reducing morbidity and mortality. Limitations The scoping review did not evaluate study quality, focusing solely on addressing the research question. The review is constrained by the included sources, and conclusions should be interpreted given these limitations. A comprehensive search was performed; however certain relevant studies, including grey literature, may have been inadvertently omitted due to the specific selection criteria, such as English language exclusivity, databases searched, employed search strings, and inherent limitations of the research process. To mitigate potential omissions and selection bias, the research team developed comprehensive search strings, using these search strings across multiple databases. Additionally, two reviewers independently selected the final articles for inclusion. Conclusion Conducting a scoping review allowed researchers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the existing literature on competencies required by EMD staff. The key finding from this review underscores the scarcity of evidence regarding the specific needs of EMD staff and the factors critical to their optimal performance. Current literature suggests that there are several competencies required by EMD staff for effective call taking and dispatching of limited resources. These competencies are critical for accurate information gathering, decision making, and appropriate resource allocation. Future research should prioritise the identification of core EMD staff competencies and how best to structure training programs to ensure their attainment. This is particularly important in LMICs where resource scarcity necessitates optimal resource allocation. Notably, the scoping review revealed a significant gap in research conducted within LMICs. To address this gap, further investigation into the unique needs of EMD in LMICs, is essential. Identifying specific competency requirements will facilitate the design of standardized training and education curricula for EMS call takers and dispatchers. 1. Introduction Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) involve the dilation of the vessel caliber, with the aortic diameter thresholds adapting to physical measurements, such as height and weight [ , ]. In addition to the etiology involving inflammatory and infectious diseases or risk factors, such as hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, genetic factors implicated in the physiopathology of vascular wall syndromes have gained significant importance in recent years, leading to improved classification and management of aortic aneurysms [ , ]. The latest AHA Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease recommend routine genetic testing of patients diagnosed with thoracic aortic aneurysm at a young age or having features associated with specific syndromes; additionally, DNA sequencing should be performed on known at-risk relatives of individuals with positive results [ ]. FTAAs are caused by their association with variants of either extracellular matrix protein function or vascular smooth muscle proteins [ ]. TAAs can be divided into two main subtypes depending on multiorgan damage, the branches being referred to as syndromic or non-syndromic. The syndromic ones include diseases affecting both the vascular system and other connective tissue abnormalities, the most notable examples of this group being Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Marfan syndrome, or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Conversely, non-syndromic TAAs are defined by their impact solely on the cardiovascular system [ ]. The pathogenic genes involved in the pathway of FTAAs affect proteins that ensure the integrity of the vascular wall, particularly vascular smooth muscle cells. Multiple genes can determine a familial pattern of thoracic aortic aneurysms, most of them having autosomal dominant inheritance, with the highest studied and prominently featured in the academic field being ACTA2 , MYH11 , MYLK , PRKG1 , and those involved in the TGF-β pathway [ , ]. Pathogenic variants of the ACTA2 gene, which encodes α-actin, are some of the most frequent etiologies of FTAAs. Alpha-actin expresses almost half of the total proteins in smooth muscle cells (up to 40%), thus making it the most representative protein at this level [ ]. In addition to cardiovascular disorders, pathogenic variants of the ACTA-2 gene predispose patients to other forms of vascular pathologies, including Moyamoya-like occlusions that can lead to early onset of cerebrovascular events or occlusions of internal carotid arteries or intracranial aneurysms [ , , ]. On the other hand, the reported case is one with complex particularities, with several medical specialties being involved and both the patient’s genetic and infectious pathology leading to consequences in the cardiovascular system. The infectious disease that the patient contracted during the last few years was an infection with Coxiella burnetii . This micro-organism is the causative agent of Q fever, being intracellular gram-negative bacteria, and is usually transmitted directly from animals, like goats or sheep, or indirectly by ticks [ , ]. It has been repeatedly indicated as a potential biological threat because it can be transmitted through inhalation, it has a low infective dose, and it has environmental stability [ , ]. The acute onset of the disease manifests as a high fever and flu-like symptoms, for example, a nonproductive cough, but because of the non-specific symptoms, the treatment is not always administered on time, allowing the Q fever to turn into a chronic disease [ , ]. The only method of preventing the disease is through immunization achieved by the Q-vax vaccine, but it is currently only administered in Australia [ ]. The most common manifestation of chronic Q fever is blood culture-negative infective endocarditis, but in some cases, the onset form may be represented by hepatitis, osteomyelitis, febrile illness lasting up to fifty days, and even neurological pathology, characterized by encephalitis, meningitis, or peripheral neuropathy [ , ]. The specific treatment of Coxiella burnetii infection is the administration of Doxycycline for 14 days for the acute infection, but in the case of chronic Q fever, a combination of Doxycycline and Hydroxychloroquine should be administered for up to 18 months [ , ]. According to the 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis, blood culture-negative infective endocarditis caused by Coxiella burnetii should be treated with Doxycycline 200 mg/24 h and Hydroxychloroquine 200–600 mg/24 h for a minimum of 18 months [ ]. 2. The following keywords were used to maximize search accuracy: “ Coxiella burnetii infection”, “Q fever”, “mechanical aortic valve”, and “blood culture-negative infective endocarditis” for the first part of the review, and “familial thoracic aortic aneurysm”, “ ACTA2 variant/mutation”, “aortic dissection”, and “ ACTA2 gene”, for the second part. The keywords were selected to improve research accuracy and capture the intricate pathologies described in our case report. The MeSH function on PubMed was used to increase the specificity of the research by using combinations of the keywords. The discovered articles were added to the Zotero application, with the ones identified as duplicates being removed. We used Microsoft 365 (Office) software, Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed in the Center for Genomic Medicine, Timișoara, for the patient and one daughter in a panel of 174 genes, using the Illumina TruSight Cardio Sequencing Panel kit and a MiSeq Illumina sequencing platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). End-to-end bioinformatics algorithms were implemented, using Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWAAligner), SAMtools, Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK-Variant Caller-Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA) and Annovar (as described elsewhere) [ ]. Alignment of the sequenced fragments was performed on the human reference genome GRCh37. A tertiary data analysis was performed at the level of current knowledge using online databases and aggregators, including Varsome, ClinVar, gnomAD, DECIPHER, UCSC Genome Browser, OMlM, DGV, and Ensembl. Results The reported case describes a 45-year-old woman known to have multiple cardiovascular conditions and a positive family history, namely her mother died at 36 years old of unknown causes (a possible spontaneous carotid artery dissection). The patient developed acute aortic dissection DeBakey type I during her second pregnancy, which was treated surgically with a Bentall procedure in 2006 by replacing the aortic valve and the ascending aorta with a valved composite graft with re-implantation of the coronary arteries into the graft. The clinical evolution of the patient was favorable for the first 15 years, followed only by chronic anticoagulant treatment of Acenocumarol 4 mg, adjusted according to the INR test. In December 2021, she started developing prolonged febrile syndrome, which was extensively investigated and treated with antibiotics several times. For two years, the patient was hospitalized in various clinics, and sets of blood cultures were performed repeatedly, all with negative results. After all the investigations were carried out, the established diagnoses were blood culture-negative infective endocarditis on the mechanical aortic valve, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated systemic vasculitis, chronic glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome form) with splenic infarction, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. In June 2024, the patient was admitted to our clinic for suspected intermittent febrile syndrome with subfebrile onset for about 3 months, accompanied by vertigo. The medical examination revealed normal vital signs and pale skin, and the cardiac examination highlighted a systolic murmur, heard loudest in the aortic area with a closing click. The ECG was normal. The pathological blood samples collected at admission revealed an inflammatory syndrome, i.e., highly elevated ESR and C-reactive protein, with positive procalcitonin. The transthoracic echocardiography showed an apparently normal mechanical prosthesis in the aortic position, mild intraprosthetic aortic regurgitation, mild mitral regurgitation, mild functional tricuspid regurgitation, mild secondary pulmonary hypertension, and a roughly 12 mm echo-dense mass surrounding the ascending aorta, also visible on the transesophageal echocardiography, as seen in . Transesophageal echocardiography provides additional information on heart morphology, usually being used for a better view of the left atrium and the left atrial appendage in order to detect thrombi, but in our case, it was used for a better view of the aortic valve [ , ]. On the second day after admission, the patient experienced a subfebrile episode, which prompted the collection of blood cultures, but the results were negative. Consequently, more specific investigations were performed, and serological tests for infective endocarditis of diverse etiology were acquired, including IgG and IgM antibodies for Mycoplasma pneumoniae , Bartonella henselae , Chlamydophila pneumoniae , Brucella spp., Legionella pneumophila , and Coxiella burnetii . All results were negative, except for Coxiella burnetii IgG and IgM phase I and phase II antibodies, and the results of both the phase I and phase II immunofluorescent assay (IFA) highlighted increased antibody titers, as seen in . Likewise, the PCR for Coxiella burnetii in the blood by molecular hybridization with an amplification test also revealed a positive result. Therefore, the diagnosis of acute onset of chronic Q fever as a disease was confirmed, the targeted therapy with Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg tid and Doxycycline 100 mg bid was initiated, and treatment will continue to be administered for 18 months. A relevant reference is the patient’s travel history; starting from 2021, the patient had not traveled abroad, and no direct link could be made to a potential source of infection, such as domestic animals. However, from 2006 to 2011, the patient traveled to several African countries for about 3 months/year, and starting in 2012, she traveled several times to Switzerland and Germany. Consequently, with the echocardiographic images revealing a significant peri-aortic mass, it was decided to perform further investigations. The thorax CT scan detected a multiloculated right semi-circumferential fluid accumulation with iodophilic walls that extends from the level of the aortic valve along the aortic prosthesis to the anterior mediastinum, suggesting a peri-aortic abscess, as seen in . Pericardial and pleural fluid collection and mediastinal adenopathies were also found. The preliminary diagnosis was Coxiella burnetii infective endocarditis complicated with mediastinal abscess; thus, a multidisciplinary team, consisting of a cardiologist, cardiovascular surgeon, infectionist, and intensive care physician, decided that the optimal management in this case would be a surgical redo operation with antibiotic protection. The surgery involved the removal of the periaortic fluid mass, with the macroscopic examination suggesting a liquefied chronic hematoma that can be seen in . The bacteriological examination of the collected biological products, pericardial fragment, periprosthetic and subprosthetic tissue, and clot fragment revealed no bacterial or fungal growth on the inoculated culture media. The post-operative evolution was favorable, and the investigations continued with genetic tests. Genetic testing for a familial aortopathy was proposed considering the positive family history of early cardiovascular-related death, the patient’s mother having passed away at the age of 36, possibly due to a spontaneous carotid artery dissection. The patient’s onset of the aortic pathology manifested as thoracic aortic dissection at the age of 27, which also constituted one of the factors that prompted the suspicion of a hereditary condition, thereby leading to genetic testing. A missense variant (variant NM_001613.4 :c.773G>A, NP_001604.1 :p.(Arg258His)) was detected in heterozygous status in the ACTA2 gene located on chromosome 10q23.31. This variant was identified in several individuals with FTAAs, segregated by phenotype. The variant was classified with pathogenic significance according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guideline [ ]. As a result, the suspicion of a genetic disease was confirmed, establishing the diagnosis of familial thoracic aortic aneurysm 6, part of a non-syndromic FTAA cluster. In some cases, the pathogenic variant of ACTA2 is associated with intracranial aneurysms and Moyamoya-like cerebrovascular disease, so the patient will be undergoing a cranial CT scan [ ]. Subsequently, her two daughters are proposed to be genetically tested and will have follow-up echocardiographic examinations. To provide a better perspective on the patient’s clinical status, paraclinical data, personal and family medical histories, and the treatment have been summarized in . The patient was discharged with a good general condition and the following diagnosis: blood culture-negative infective endocarditis with Coxiella burnetii , liquefied chronic periprosthetic hematoma (surgically treated), status post-Bentall operation, normofunctional double disc mechanical prosthesis in the aortic position, mild mitral regurgitation, mild functional tricuspid regurgitation, mild secondary pulmonary hypertension, NYHA I chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis, chronic glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome form), enlarged spleen with subcapsular infarction, and mild normochromic normocytic anemia, and the following treatment being recommended at home: Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/tid, Doxycycline 100 mg bid, Acenocoumarol 4 mg (dose controlled by INR test in order to maintain a value between 2.5–3.5), diuretics

blood culture-negative infective endocarditis with Coxiella burnetii , liquefied chronic periprosthetic hematoma (surgically treated), status post-Bentall operation, normofunctional double disc mechanical prosthesis in the aortic position, mild mitral regurgitation, mild functional tricuspid regurgitation, mild secondary pulmonary hypertension, NYHA I chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis, chronic glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome form), enlarged spleen with subcapsular infarction, and mild normochromic normocytic anemia, and the following treatment being recommended at home: Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/tid, Doxycycline 100 mg bid, Acenocoumarol 4 mg (dose controlled by INR test in order to maintain a value between 2.5–3.5), diuretics (association between Furosemide/Spironolactone 20/50 mg/day), and a probiotic. The specific antibiotic treatment for Coxiella burnetii BCNIE with Hydroxychloroquine and Doxycycline will be administered for 18 months, according to the 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis. This approach is tailored to the patient’s clinical course, the prolonged progression of febrile syndrome with multiple recurrences, and the potential complications that could be associated with mediastinal spread of the infection [ ]. The only side effects reported by the patient regarding the specific medication for Coxiella burnetii were insomnia and tinnitus. 4. Discussion In order to perform an accurate review starting with the reported case, which included two major significant pathologies, both a genetically inherited disease, the ACTA2 variant gene leading to a familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, as well as a rare infectious disease, namely blood culture-negative infective endocarditis on a mechanical aortic valve, the research on the medical literature started by looking for the coexistence of both pathologies, but it failed to identify any patient similar to the case presented above. Therefore, our research was oriented toward searching separately for the two intricate pathologies, the review encompassing medical articles describing, on one hand, blood culture-negative infective endocarditis with Coxiella burnetii on a mechanical aortic valve and, on the other hand, studies presenting patients having familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and/or dissection due to the ACTA2 disease-causing variant. Firstly, in the interest of achieving similarities between the described patient’s infectious disease with cardiovascular implications and the patients included in the chosen studies, we identified articles published in the medical literature between 2000 and August 2024 available on PubMed and ResearchGate. The inclusion criteria that the selected articles had to meet were patients with a medical history including a surgery replacing the native aortic valve with a prosthetic one; patients diagnosed with Coxiella burnetii blood culture-negative infective endocarditis; studies including clear diagnosis and management parameters and having an explicit outcome for the patients; articles published in the target period of time; and studies defined as case reports. The exclusion criteria were studies published before 2000; studies having qualities other than case reports; articles that did not include accurate patient management details; and studies including non-human participants. The research strategy was designed using keywords and phrases closely relevant to the reported case; thus, the keywords included “ Coxiella burnetii infection”, “Q fever”, “mechanical aortic valve”, and “blood culture-negative infective endocarditis”. There were four identified case reports describing Coxiella burnetii -associated blood culture-negative infective endocarditis on a prosthetic aortic valve, as seen in . The most frequently described symptom in these patients was fever, and, in most of the cases, febrile symptomatology started about a month before the presentation. In our patient, fever was present for about two and a half years, with periods of remission, subfebrility, or aggravation episodes. The treatment in two of the cases was exclusively medical, one patient benefited from surgical intervention, and one case was managed through both medical and surgical therapy. One case was treated with a special antibiotic, as Afrasiabian et al. [ ] described intolerance to Doxycycline, and thus the antibiotic treatment chosen instead was levofloxacin. Krol et al. [ ] also preferred the administration of monotherapy with Doxycycline for 5 months, leading to a favorable result and an improved patient outcome. The treatment preferred by Bozza et al. [ ] was the administration of Doxycycline 100 mg/bid in association with Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/tid for 24 months, with a long-term follow-up of the patient, which proved the efficacy of the chosen antibiotics through a decreasing trend in the serological tests. This combination of antibiotics was also chosen for the patient treated in our clinic, being well tolerated by the patient, without fever remissions. The characteristics of the Coxiella burnetii infection selected to compare with the patient’s evolution described in our case report with the literature data represent only a subset of the features associated with this complex disease. Coxiella burnetii is defined as an intracellular bacterium causing a zoonotic disease transmitted from animals like sheep, cattle, or goats to humans, with ticks being the main reservoir in nature. The transmission is usually performed through aerosols, but vertical, transplacental, or even nosocomial infection is also possible.

The characteristics of the Coxiella burnetii infection selected to compare with the patient’s evolution described in our case report with the literature data represent only a subset of the features associated with this complex disease. Coxiella burnetii is defined as an intracellular bacterium causing a zoonotic disease transmitted from animals like sheep, cattle, or goats to humans, with ticks being the main reservoir in nature. The transmission is usually performed through aerosols, but vertical, transplacental, or even nosocomial infection is also possible. In humans, the infection may present many forms, including an asymptomatic course or progression through two distinct phases, acute and chronic disease. Acute infection can manifest as febrile symptomatology or flu-like onset, but it may also appear as hepatitis, pneumonia, or other manifestations. The presence and duration of fever were included in the comparative characteristics evaluated in the patients analyzed in this review. The most common manifestation of chronic Q fever is endocarditis; however, hepatitis, ophthalmological or neurological disorders, and infections of vascular grafts may also be present as forms of the disease. In addition, a second part of the research was the comparison of the patient’s evolution regarding the aortic disease caused by the ACTA2 variant with the patients described in the chosen articles. The research among the medical literature provided five case reports published between 2000 and August 2024 that describe patients having a thoracic aortic aneurysm with a positive family history and the ACTA2 variant, as seen in . The inclusion criteria were patients presenting any type of variant of the ACTA2 gene expressing vascular smooth muscle cells; studies having the quality of case reports; and studies providing clear evidence of patient management. On the other hand, the exclusion criteria were studies involving non-human participants; studies published before the year 2000; and studies with characteristics other than case reports. The examination was conducted among the studies found on PubMed and ResearchGate. The prevalence of the targeted aortic pathology was found to be higher among men, with 57.1% of the patients described in the selected studies being males. Similarly, the ACTA2 disease-causing variant genes were discovered to be more frequent among males with aortic disease. Concerning the average age of patients with familial thoracic aortic aneurysm, the oldest patient experiencing acute onset of the condition was 41 years old, as described by Hoffjan et al. [ ], while the youngest was just 15 years old, namely the study published by Ware et al. [ ] presenting the twins who developed acute aortic dissection at the same time. In the patients’ family history, cases carrying the mutant gene were identified after genetic counseling and testing because they did not experience any clinical manifestation of the disease. Similar to the reported data in the literature, our patient’s clinical onset was very early; the acute aortic dissection occurred at the age of 27. Among the included patients, only two of them presented a notable phenotypic manifestation, namely congenital mydriasis in the twins described by Ware et al. [ ]. This clinical expression was also described in the specialized literature as being strongly associated with a particular missense variant in arginine 179 in the ACTA2 gene [ ]. The complexity of the reported case arises from the early onset of the aortic disease, the patient being 7 months pregnant when she presented at the hospital for acute aortic dissection. This circumstance is consistent with the documented data regarding the evolution of pregnancies in females with the ACTA2 variant [ ]. Thus, Hoffjan et al. [ ] described two patients with a history of physiological pregnancy before being diagnosed with mild aortic dilation and acute aortic dissection. The academic literature describes a powerful connection between an underlying aortic disease and an aortic dissection associated with pregnancy. Fluctuations in pregnancy hormone levels, along with the hemodynamic stress experienced by pregnant women, can exacerbate a subjacent aortic condition, particularly during the third trimester [ ]. Furthermore, genetic counseling should be the standard practice in all the cases outlined above. This management step is crucial for families where one member has already been identified for the ACTA2 disease-causing variant, as this gene is associated with an increased risk of vascular diseases, as seen in every presented study. Considering the autosomal dominant transmission of the ACTA2 gene, each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant; thus, the two daughters of the patient presented in our case report will undergo genetic counseling to facilitate future cardiovascular follow-up and ensure that any potential complication can be managed in time. Considering the autosomal dominant transmission of the ACTA2 gene, each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant; thus, the two daughters of the patient presented in our case report will undergo genetic counseling to facilitate future cardiovascular follow-up and ensure that any potential complication can be managed in time. If a child is found to be a hereditary carrier, management strategies should focus on regular cardiovascular monitoring through echocardiograms or CT scans and implementing lifestyle changes that minimize stress on the cardiovascular system. This might include controlling blood pressure and avoiding heavy lifting or other risk factors, such as smoking. Pregnancy will be monitored closely as it adds additional stress to the aorta. In some cases, preventive surgical options might be discussed if imaging indicates a high risk of vascular events. In addition to medical information, genetic counseling addresses the emotional impact of a genetic diagnosis, providing resources and support for the psychological aspects of living with an inherited condition. Discussing the options for preimplantation genetic or prenatal testing of the ACTA2 variant is included in the genetic counseling. 5. Conclusions To summarize, a familial thoracic aortic aneurysm is a condition with a high mortality rate if it is not properly diagnosed and monitored over time. These findings should encourage more frequent genetic testing in patients with aortic aneurysms, especially those with significant familial medical history or an early onset of the aortic disease. Additionally, a condition of particular importance but meaningful diagnostic and therapeutical challenges is blood culture-negative infective endocarditis. Rare causes should be investigated, and serological testing for infectious agents such as Coxiella burnetii ought to be considered. The management of a patient with both a genetic variant already manifested through a cardiovascular complication and a concurrent infectious disease is very particular due to the complexity of the case and requires a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach focused on surveillance and proactive care. Therefore, regular cardiovascular imaging, blood pressure monitoring, and infection status assessment are essential to detect early signs of complications. Genetic counseling and family screening may also be beneficial for identifying at-risk relatives, enabling timely follow-up.

chunks.content: KEY POINTS Question: Does hyperoxia during venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support increase the risk of acute brain injury (ABI) and in-hospital mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock? Findings: Pa o 2 ≥150 mm Hg at 4/24 hours post-ECMO predicted ABI, while Pa o 2 ≥300 mm Hg at 24 hours predicted mortality. Meaning: Avoiding hyperoxia during VA-ECMO support may reduce the risk of ABI and in-hospital mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock. Over the past 10 years, the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for patients experiencing persistent cardiogenic shock (CS) has increased rapidly. – VA-ECMO provides both temporary mechanical circulatory support and extracorporeal gas exchange through a membrane oxygenator and can serve as a bridge to recovery or to other mechanical support strategies. Because blood flowing through the VA-ECMO circuit does not pass through the patient’s lungs, it must be oxygenated before returning to the arterial circulation and mixing with the patient’s native circulation. Consequently, patients on VA-ECMO are frequently managed with varying degrees of hyperoxia, and existing data suggest that higher levels of Pao₂ correlate with worsened outcomes. Currently, little guidance is available with respect to the resulting arterial Pa o 2 for patients receiving VA-ECMO therapy. While hypoxia is clearly detrimental, hyperoxia, characterized by supranormal oxygen levels in the blood, can increase reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and predispose to lung injury, reduced organ blood flow, impaired kidney and liver function, heightened risks of blood clotting, immune suppression, and cellular damage. , Hyperoxia has also been associated with increased mortality rates in patients suffering from refractory CS, and negatively affects outcomes in several critical conditions. The recent Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) Interim Guidelines for VA-ECMO emphasize avoiding both excessive hypo- and hyperoxia and recommend that the post-oxygenator Pa 0 2 in patients on ECMO should be titrated to 150 mm Hg. A 2022 review of the ELSO registry found that elevated Pa o 2 levels correlated with poorer outcomes in cardiac arrest (CA) patients who received extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). A similar 2023 review found that hyperoxia is incrementally associated with higher rates of in-hospital mortality and lower rates of native heart survival from the ELSO registry. Several other studies have also reported that hyperoxia during VA-ECMO has adverse effects on patient prognosis. – However, a 2017 study found no increase in the rate of acute brain injury (ABI) or in-hospital mortality in hyperoxia patients on VA-ECMO. In patients on ECMO, ABI is common with published incidences ranging from 8% to 50%. – ABI may occur from global brain ischemia during CA or CS, or after ECMO initiation when rapid restoration of cerebral blood flow can lead to reperfusion injury. , A 2023 review of 3125 patients from the ELSO registry found that severe hyperoxia (Pa 0 2 ≥300 mm Hg) after ECMO initiation was associated with ABI and increased mortality. ABI is a major contributor morbidity and a predictor of higher mortality rates in ECMO patients. Given the critical condition and high mortality risk in this patient population, early clinical assessment is paramount for outcome prediction. Therefore, we focused our analysis on the association between oxygenation status during the initial phase of ECMO support and subsequent clinical outcomes. We hypothesized that hyperoxia (Pa 0 2 ≥150 mm Hg) during VA-ECMO support is associated with an increased risk of ABI and in-hospital mortality in patients with CS. This study aimed to investigate these associations while accounting for potential confounders. METHODS Study Population This retrospective cohort study, conducted at Beijing Anzhen Hospital, Capital Medical University (January 2017–July 2024), icluded adults (≥18 years) receiving VA-ECMO for CS, indentified using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) code (ICD-9: 785.51/ICD-10: R57.1). The study protocol (2019040X) was approved by the Institutional Ethics Review Committee, which waived the requirement for informed consent due to the retrospective nature of this study. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. Exclusion criteria comprised: (1) ECMO duration <24 hours; (2) ECPR or combined ECMO modalities; (3) pre-ECMO hyperoxia (Pa o ₂ >200 mm Hg). The study design is presented in Figure . ECMO Implantation and Management All patients received VA-ECMO support via peripheral cannulation. Specifically, the semiopen method was used for femoral venous and arterial access. To prevent severe lower limb ischemia, a distal perfusion catheter was inserted into the femoral artery. All procedures were performed by a trained ECMO team, with ECMO blood flow adjusted according to clinical evaluations. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was administered to maintain an activated clotting time (ACT) of 180–210 seconds or an activated partial thromboplastin time 1.5–2 times the baseline value. Arterial blood samples for oxygen content analysis were obtained from the right radial artery, in accordance with the ELSO guidelines recommendation for monitoring arterial blood gases (ABGs) during ECMO support. All procedures were performed by a trained ECMO team, with ECMO blood flow adjusted according to clinical evaluations. Intravenous unfractionated heparin was administered to maintain an activated clotting time (ACT) of 180–210 seconds or an activated partial thromboplastin time 1.5–2 times the baseline value. Arterial blood samples for oxygen content analysis were obtained from the right radial artery, in accordance with the ELSO guidelines recommendation for monitoring arterial blood gases (ABGs) during ECMO support. Data Collection and Definitions We collected baseline characteristics, medical history, hemodynamic parameters, pulse pressure, and ABG values before and after ECMO initiation (referred to as “pre-ECMO” and “on-ECMO,” respectively). The pre-ECMO ABG value and pre-ECMO pulse pressure refer to the worst measurement recorded within the 6 hours before ECMO initiation. ABG measurements were collected at 2 predefined time points: 4 hours (±10 minutes) and 24 hours (±10 minutes) after ECMO initiation. ΔPa o 2 was calculated as the difference between 24-hour post-ECMO and pre-ECMO Pa o 2 values. We defined 3 categories of pre-ECMO Pa o 2 values: hypoxemia (<60 mm Hg), normoxia (60–149 mm Hg), mild hyperoxia (150–200 mm Hg) and 4 categories of post-ECMO Pa o 2 values: normoxia (60–149 mm Hg), mild hyperoxia (150–199 mm Hg), moderate hyperoxia (200–299 mm Hg), and severe hyperoxia (≥300 mm Hg). ABI was defined as having one or more of the following: ischemic stroke (IS), intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI), or neurological examination abnormalities (NEA). IS was defined as central nervous system (CNS) infarction confirmed by ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). ICH was defined as intra- or extraparenchymal CNS hemorrhage confirmed by CT or MRI. The diagnosis of HIBI included cerebral changes characteristic of ischemic-hypoxic encephalopathy, as demonstrated by imaging studies such as MRI or CT scans, including brain swelling, abnormal areas of low blood flow, or infarcts (regions of tissue death). NEA were defined as altered mental status, motor and sensory deficits, coordination problems, gait abnormalities, reflex abnormalities, cranial nerve dysfunction, seizures, visual or auditory impairments, and speech and language disorders, all of which may indicate underlying neurological conditions during VA-ECMO support. ABI assessment and diagnosis were performed during the ECMO run period, preceding any weaning attempts or circuit discontinuation. Outcomes The primary outcome was the composite incidence of ABI, defined as the occurrence of any of the following subtypes: IS + ICH, HIBI, and NEA. The secondary outcomes were the individual incidence of each ABI type. Other outcomes were in-hospital mortality, 60-day mortality. Statistical Analysis Categorical variables are presented as frequencies (percentages), and comparisons between groups were performed using the χ 2 test. Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median [interquartile range], and group comparisons were conducted using the independent samples t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test, as appropriate. For comparisons among multiple groups, the Kruskal-Wallis H test was used. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 1.4.1103, with a significance level set at P < .05. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression were performed to determine associations between Pa o 2 category and (1) composite ABI, (2) IS + ICH, (3) HIBI, (4) NEA, and (5) in-hospital mortality. A linear mixed-effects model was used to compare Pa o 2 levels between ABI and non-ABI groups at 4 and 24 hours post-ECMO initiation, with a random intercept for individual patients. The model incorporated group, timepoint, and their interaction as fixed effects. Between-group differences were assessed using Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, with statistical significance defined as P < .05 (2-tailed). Variables with a P value of <.05 in the univariable analysis were included in the multivariable regression model; variables with Pearson’s correlation coefficients >0.7 were excluded to avoid multicollinearity. Remaining variables with variance inflation factors (VIF) <5 were entered into the multivariable logistic regression model. Adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to identify independent risk factors. A P value of <.05 was considered statistically significant. The association between ΔPa o ₂ categories and ABI incidence was assessed using the Cochran-Armitage trend test. A statistically significant trend ( P < .05) would indicate a monotonic increase in ABI incidence across ordered ΔPa o ₂ categories. To assess the consistency between individual ABI subtypes and the composite ABI outcome, we performed reliability analysis using Cohen’s Kappa statistic. Sequential exclusion of individual ABI subtypes evaluated their independent outcome contributions. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was used to evaluate the 60-day survival outcomes across different Pa o 2 classifications, with between-group differences tested by log-rank ( P < .05 significant). Two hundred thirty-two patients did not meet the inclusion criteria and were excluded. Ultimately, 481 patients were included in the present study. Demographic information and patient characteristics are presented in Table . There were 317 (65.9%) and 164 (34.1%) patients involved in the non-ABI and ABI groups, respectively. The type of ABI was IS + ICH (n = 73, 44.5%), HIBI (n = 25, 5.20%), and NEA (n = 66, 13.72%). Figure shows the distribution of Pa 0 2 levels at 24 hours post-ECMO initiation in the study cohort. The mean Pao 2 after 24 hours on ECMO was 164 mm Hg. Based on our study definitions, 262 (54.5%) patients had normoxia, 80 (16.63%) had mild hyperoxia, 92 (19.1%) had moderate hyperoxia, and 47 (9.77%) had severe hyperoxia (Table ). Arterial Oxygen Pressure and ABI Patients with ABI exhibited a lower mean pre-ECMO Pa 0 2 compared to those without ABI (78.8 vs 90.4 mm Hg; P = .004), as shown in Table . ABI patients demonstrated significantly higher Pa o ₂ levels than non-ABI patients at both 4 hours (mean difference 108 mm Hg; 95% CI, 87.7–127) and 24 hours post-ECMO (61.9 mm Hg; 95% CI, 42.1–81.8; both P < .001) (Supplemental Digital Content 1, Table S1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F502 ). The majority of patients with composite ABI and its subtypes were exposed to a high Pa o 2 , as illustrated in Supplemental Digital Content 2, Table S2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F503 , and Figure . All subtypes of ABI patients exhibited a higher Pa o 2 at 24 hours on ECMO compared to non-ABI patients. Patients with Pa o 2 exceeding 150 mm Hg had a significantly higher likelihood of developing ABI compared to those with lower Pa o 2 levels after both univariable and multivariate logistic regression analyses (Table ; Figure ). Patients with oxygen partial pressure levels between 200 and 299 mm Hg had the highest incidence of ABI compared to those with other oxygen partial pressure levels. Supplemental Digital Content 3, Figure S1, https://links.lww.com/AA/F504 , illustrates the prevalence of ABI and non-ABI cases across different ΔPa o ₂ ranges. A significant dose–response relationship was observed between ΔPa o ₂ intervals and ABI incidence ( P for trend <.001). The ABI rate progressively increased from 13.0% in the lowest ΔPa o ₂ stratum (–150 to –50 mm Hg) to 61.4% in the highest stratum (>150 mm Hg), with intermediate rates of 17.9% (–50 to 50 mm Hg) and 44.0% (50–150 mm Hg). This trend remained statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounders (Supplemental Digital Content 4, Table S3, https://links.lww.com/AA/F505 ). Neurological Examination Abnormalities According to the multivariable logistic regression model (Supplemental Digital Content 9, Table S8, https://links.lww.com/AA/F510 ), age (OR, 1.03; 95% CI, 1.00–1.05), mild hyperoxia (OR, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.24–5.98), moderate hyperoxia (OR, 3.61; 95% CI, 1.75–7.45), and severe hyperoxia (OR, 3.17; 95% CI, 1.26–7.96) were connected with NEA in ECMO duration. Subgroup Sensitivity Analyses for ABI Components Among 164 ABI patients, IS + ICH (44.6%) and NEA (40.2%) constituted the majority, while HIBI was less frequent (15.2%, Supplemental Digital Content 10, Table S9, https://links.lww.com/AA/F511 ). Inter-rater reliability analysis revealed moderate agreement for IS + ICH ( κ = 0.51) and NEA ( κ = 0.47), but poor agreement for HIBI classification ( κ = 0.19) (Supplemental Digital Content 11, Table S10, https://links.lww.com/AA/F512 ). To assess the weight distribution of the composite outcome (ABI), we performed sensitivity analysis using a stepwise exclusion method, sequentially removing each ABI subtype and re-running multivariate regression (Supplemental Digital Content 12, Table S11, https://links.lww.com/AA/F513 ). The results showed that hyperoxia (Pa o ₂≥150 mm Hg) at both 4- and 24-hour time points significantly increased ABI risk (OR, 2.33–6.10; all P < .05). However, this association was markedly attenuated after excluding either NEA or IS + ICH, while excluding HIBI had minimal impact on overall risk estimates. Further analysis revealed that the risk trends of NEA and IS + ICH subgroups were highly consistent with the composite ABI outcome, whereas HIBI contributed relatively less. Additionally, elevated lactate levels (Lac) were significantly associated with NEA (OR, 1.08; P = .007) but showed a negative association with HIBI (OR, 0.93; P = .029). The sensitivity analysis confirmed that the risk of composite ABI was primarily driven by NEA and IS + ICH, with HIBI having a relatively weak independent effect. In-hospital Mortality and Arterial Oxygen Pressure In the total population, the number of deaths was 281 (58.4%); mortality in the moderate and severe hyperoxia groups was higher than in the normoxia group (Supplemental Digital Content 13, Table S12, https://links.lww.com/AA/F514 and Supplemental Digital Content 14, Figure S2, https://links.lww.com/AA/F515 ). After multivariable logistic regression, severe hyperoxia (OR, 2.46; 95% CI, 1.25–4.84) and Lac (OR, 1.00; 95% CI, 1.02–1.25) at ECMO on 24 hours were identified as independent risk factor for in-hospital mortality. The use of IABP (OR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.31–0.82) and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT; OR, 2.46; 95% CI, 1.25–4.84) were associated with a lower in-hospital mortality (Supplemental Digital Content 15, Table S13, https://links.lww.com/AA/F516 ). ABI and In-hospital Mortality Patients with ABI demonstrated significantly higher mortality than non-ABI cases (85.4% vs 44.5%; P < .001), with all ABI subtypes exhibiting mortality rates exceeding 80% (Tables and ). These findings underscore the critical prognostic impact of ABI. 60-Day Mortality and Arterial Oxygen Pressure At 24 hours post-ECMO initiation, significant differences in 60-day survival were observed among oxygenation groups (log-rank test, P = .044; Figure ). Patients with mild hyperoxia demonstrated a median survival time of 14.0 days (95% CI, 8.58–19.4), while those with moderate hyperoxia showed a median survival of 9.01 days (95% CI, 6.04–12.0). In contrast, severe hyperoxia was associated with substantially shorter median survival (4.50 days; 95% CI, 0–10.3) (Supplemental Digital Content 16, Table S14, https://links.lww.com/AA/F517 ). The normoxia group exhibited the most favorable outcomes, with survival probability remaining above 50% throughout the 60-day observation period (median not estimable). DISCUSSION In our retrospective analysis of 481 patients receiving VA-ECMO support, we observed a dose-dependent association between hyperoxia during the first 24 hours and both ABI incidence (34.10%) and in-hospital mortality. Among confirmed ABI cases, IS + ICH (44.5%) predominated, while HIBI was least frequent. Both hyperoxia at 4- and 24-hour post-ECMO initiation significantly increased the risk of adverse outcomes, with a graded dose–response relationship observed across severity levels of hyperoxia. Multivariate analysis revealed elevated lactate level during ECMO as an independent predictor of adverse outcome. Our study extends this evidence by introducing rapid Pa o ₂ elevation as novel risk modifiers. Patients with greater oxygen level increases (ΔPa o ₂ >150 mm Hg) after ECMO initiation had significantly higher rates of ABI (61.4% vs 13.0% with minimal changes), demonstrating a clear dose–dependent relationship between oxygen surge magnitude and neurological risk. These findings highlight the importance of careful oxygen monitoring to prevent brain injury. Severe hyperoxia may aggravate reperfusion injury during ECMO by potentiating

Our study extends this evidence by introducing rapid Pa o ₂ elevation as novel risk modifiers. Patients with greater oxygen level increases (ΔPa o ₂ >150 mm Hg) after ECMO initiation had significantly higher rates of ABI (61.4% vs 13.0% with minimal changes), demonstrating a clear dose–dependent relationship between oxygen surge magnitude and neurological risk. These findings highlight the importance of careful oxygen monitoring to prevent brain injury. Severe hyperoxia may aggravate reperfusion injury during ECMO by potentiating toxic-free radical formation, including vasoconstriction, and increasing the likelihood of a proinflammatory state and neuronal metabolic failure. VA-ECMO delivers fully oxygenated blood into the arterial system, it can easily result in arterial hyperoxia. In a 2021 comparison of patients with CS supported by balloon pump or ECMO, the Pa o 2 in the ECMO group was 286 vs 103 mm Hg for the balloon pump group, suggesting that hyperoxia may occur commonly with VA-ECMO. The 2023 ELSO analysis demonstrated a continuous dose-response between Pa o ₂ and mortality, though lacked neurological endpoints. For ECPR patients, severe hyperoxia (Pa o ₂ ≥300 mm Hg) independently predicted ABI and death, a relationship potentially modulated by anoxic injury in CA cohorts. , , – Our sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the composite ABI outcome, with IS + ICH ( κ = 0.51) and NEA ( κ = 0.47) showing moderate agreement, while HIBI ( κ = 0.19) contributed minimally. This conclusion is supported by 3 key findings: (1) exclusion of NEA/IS + ICH significantly reduced the OR values for hyperoxia; (2) lactate levels showed positive correlation with NEA (OR, 1.08) but negative correlation with HIBI (OR, 0.93); (3) the low agreement in HIBI diagnosis suggests potential observer variability and pathological heterogeneity in its imaging-based assessment. These findings have important clinical implications: oxygenation management strategies should be optimized for NEA and IS + ICH, while multimodal evaluation incorporating biomarkers is recommended to improve diagnostic accuracy for HIBI. Future research should focus on establishing more precise imaging diagnostic criteria for HIBI and developing subtype-specific individualized treatment protocols. This study provides evidence-based support for the precise classification and management of ABI. These findings underscore the critical need for stringent oxygenation protocols during VA-ECMO, with the following key clinical priorities: (1) closely monitoring the magnitude of Pa o ₂ fluctuations, as rapid increases may compromise cerebral autoregulation; (2) enhanced neurological surveillance is recommended for patients exhibiting early hyperoxia after ECMO initiation. Because in our cohort, hyperoxia on ECMO was associated with both our composite ABI outcome and all ABI subtypes. Limitations and Future Directions Our findings demonstrate a 34% incidence of ABI in VA-ECMO patients, which aligns with the 11%–20% range reported in ELSO registry data , yet remains substantially lower than the 68%–81% incidence documented in autopsy studies. , , This retrospective analysis has several important limitations that warrant consideration. Most significantly, while we observed an association between hyperoxia and adverse outcomes, the study design cannot establish causality due to potential unmeasured confounding variables. The reliability of our neurological outcomes may be affected by the lack of standardized diagnostic adjudication and neuromonitoring protocols across participating centers, potentially leading to underestimation of true ABI rates. Furthermore, although hyperoxia showed correlation with poor outcomes in pre-ECMO CA patients, our exclusion of ECPR cases limits the generalizability of these findings to that particular population. – Several methodological constraints should be noted in the interpretation of our results. The absence of pre-ECMO neurological assessments, including standardized measures like Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, precluded comprehensive evaluation of baseline neurological status. While our study captured survival and basic neurological outcomes, more sophisticated neurocognitive testing might have revealed subtler manifestations of ABI not detected by our current assessment protocols. Additionally, the observed Pa o 2 levels reflect a complex interplay between ECMO support and native cardiac function. , This relationship is particularly evident in femoro-femoral VA-ECMO, where the balance between retrograde ECMO flow and anterograde native cardiac output at the aortic transition point results in higher ECMO-dependent Pa o 2 levels in patients with more impaired cardiac function. After rigorous adjustment for pulse pressure, hyperoxia maintained its significant association with both ABI occurrence and in-hospital mortality. However, our analysis could not account for potential confounding from ventilator management strategies, as detailed ventilator parameters and their temporal changes were not systematically recorded. Importantly, while this study establishes hyperoxia as an independent risk factor for ABI during ECMO, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. Future investigations should use integrated physiological and molecular approaches to clarify how hyperoxia mediates neurological injury in this setting, knowledge that will prove essential for developing effective neuroprotective interventions. CONCLUSIONS In our retrospective review of patients

However, our analysis could not account for potential confounding from ventilator management strategies, as detailed ventilator parameters and their temporal changes were not systematically recorded. Importantly, while this study establishes hyperoxia as an independent risk factor for ABI during ECMO, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. Future investigations should use integrated physiological and molecular approaches to clarify how hyperoxia mediates neurological injury in this setting, knowledge that will prove essential for developing effective neuroprotective interventions. CONCLUSIONS In our retrospective review of patients receiving VA-ECMO support for CS, we found that severe hyperoxia (>300 mm Hg) is progressively correlated with increased rates of ABI—whose composite risk is predominantly driven by NEA and IS + ICH—and in-hospital mortality. Based on our findings, it is possible that targeting a Pa o ₂ level below 200 mm Hg during VA-ECMO support may reduce the risks of hyperoxia-related complications. Until data from randomized clinical trials become available, it may be prudent to avoid high Pa o ₂ levels in patients with CS on VA-ECMO. DISCLOSURES Conflicts of Interest: None.
